The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. Those who study the Way should at all times keep this in mind, day and night.
How easily time passes! If one does not say "it will come," the living will fail to cultivate themselves; what will the dead possess? This greedy and vulgar habit is truly shameful.
It was for this reason that the *Miaoshan Jingce* (The Cautionary Admonition of Mount Wei) was composed. — Dinghu.

While serving as an attendant to the Master, he propagated the wondrous Way and exhorted those who came to study. His instructions were earnest, sincere, and profound, and his encouragement and support were exhaustive.

One day, the assembly requested that the Master provide an exposition on the essential principles of the *Miaofengshan Jingce* (The Warning Verses of Mount Miao). With unimpeded wisdom and eloquence, the Master [proceeded].

This delighted the hearts of the assembly. Consequently, they further requested that the Master provide a topical outline (*pī-ko*) and a word-by-word commentary (*ju-shih*), so that the purport of the exhortation might become perfectly clear.
Thus, whether one is of superior wisdom or of middling capacity, all may follow this practice to reach the ultimate Way.

The Master’s senior disciple, Monk Shijian Xiong, recorded the words of the Master’s exposition from those days and appended them to the end of each chapter, like adding flowers to brocade or oil to a lamp, thereby enhancing its brilliance.
Ming: This book is of great benefit to later students; it is no small matter.
Those who read this book will be as if they were seeing Mount Guiyang, and as if they were seeing the Master and Mount Guiyang speaking with one voice and sharing the same heart.

One can thereby infer how the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity exerted their utmost efforts for the sake of others, and how they exhorted, encouraged, and cautioned the assembly. Formerly, Da'an...
The Chan Master said: "For thirty years at Mount Gui, I watched over a water buffalo.

Now it has transformed into a white ox in an open field, always before my eyes, standing wide-eyed all day long; even if I try to drive it away, it will not go. This can truly be called being able to admonish oneself.
My wish is that all practitioners of the Way in the world shall, like Chan Master Dajian, be able to [admonish themselves].
Written by the disciple from Yu Mountain,
Kuang Yi,
at the foot of Longquan Mountain during the final watch of the twelfth month in the year Gengzi of the Shunzhi era, as he exhorted those who require such exhortation.

To explain this text, the major outline is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the main body.
Regarding the first, the explanation of the title, there are two sections: A. The Person; B. The Dharma. Under A. The Person, [the first is] Mount Guiyang.
The four characters of the title consist of two characters above that refer to the person who explains, and two characters below that refer to the Dharma being explained.
Regarding the person being designated by "Mount": the mountain is situated to the northwest of Changsha Prefecture;
because the Master resided there, he was called by the name of the mountain out of respect for him. As for the Master—
His taboo name was Lingyou; his secular surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Changxi in Fuzhou. He left home to become a monk at the age of fifteen and received full ordination at twenty.
He thoroughly investigated the sutras and vinayas of both the Mahayana and Hinayana traditions. At twenty-three, he traveled to Jiangxi to visit the Chan Master Dazhi of Baiyang.
Upon first seeing him, Baiyang granted him permission to enter the inner quarters, and he subsequently became the foremost among those engaged in study. One day...
While standing in attendance, the Master ordered him to poke the brazier and fetch some fire. The Master poked it and said, "There is no fire.
The Master himself rose and poked deeply, obtaining a small amount of fire. He held it up to show him and said, "You say there is none; what is this? Thereupon, the Master attained realization.
He prostrated in thanks and set forth what he had realized. The Master said, "This is merely a temporary crossroads. As the Sutra says:

If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and season. When the time and season arrive, it is like suddenly awakening from a dream or suddenly remembering what was forgotten;
one then realizes that one’s own property is not obtained from another. Therefore, the Patriarch said: "Awakening is the same as non-awakening;
there is no mind and there is no dharma. This simply means being without the deluded mind of ordinary people and sages; it is the original mind.
The Dharma is fundamentally complete within oneself. Now that you are thus, protect and maintain it well. Later, the Master served as the steward (dianzuo).

At that time, the Ascetic Sima came from Hunan and said to him, "Recently, while in Hunan, I found a mountain named Dayue, which is the dwelling place of a spiritual teacher (shanzhishi) who has fifteen hundred followers."
Linji said, "Would it be appropriate for this old monk to go and reside there? Deyi replied, "That is not a place for the Master to dwell.
Linji asked, "Why not? Deyi said, "The Master is a man of bone; that place is a mountain of flesh. Even if you were to reside there, your followers would never number a thousand.
Linji then ordered his attendant to summon the Head Seat and asked, "What do you think of this man? Deyi requested him to clear his throat once.
After walking several paces, Da said, "It cannot be. He then summoned the head cook to question him; upon seeing him, Da said, "This is truly the master of Mount Shuangfeng.
That night, the Abbot summoned the Master into his room and instructed him, saying, "My karmic conditions for transformation lie here.
Mount Shuangfeng is a magnificent realm; you shall dwell there, succeed my school, and extensively deliver future students. The Master then—
He went to dwell there. The mountain was steep and precipitous, with coiled trees and remote valleys extending for several hundred miles;
it was the abode of bears, leopards, tigers, and rhinoceroses, where human tracks were rarely seen. The Master took monkeys as his companions, gathering acorns and chestnuts to sustain himself.
After six or seven years, the local villagers gradually learned of him and led the masses to jointly construct a Buddhist temple. From this, the Way spread throughout the world.
Zen studies converged upon him, and he subsequently established the Guiyang school. For over forty years, he propagated the orthodox teaching;
those who attained enlightenment were beyond counting, while those who entered his inner circle numbered forty-one.

On the ninth day of the first month in the seventh year of the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, having washed and rinsed his mouth, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away with a serene expression. He was eighty-three years of age by secular reckoning; [his monastic seniority was...]
64. His stupa was erected on the southern ridge of the mountain. By imperial decree, Chan Master Dayuan was posthumously titled Chiming; his stupa was named Qingjing. The inscription states:
"According to tradition, the Master resided at Mount Gui for a long time. He himself knew that in a previous life he had been a monk reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* at a village temple in Yuezhou.
The year of the Master’s passing was one thousand eight hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata."
It has been two years since [the founding]. As for the Dharma Master Sima: internally, he secretly preserved the school of Direct Pointing;
externally, he possessed the discernment of human relations. Furthermore, he thoroughly mastered geomancy, and those establishing temples in various regions frequently sought his decision.
The Head Seat was none other than Venerable Hualin.
II. Exhortation by Means of the Two Dharmas.
These two characters constitute the essential purport of this entire fascicle. "Exhortation" (jing) means to awaken those who have not yet realized; "urging on" (ce) means...

Exhorting the later generations: At that time, the Great Master of Mount Gui, observing that the Dharma was in its final stage, saw that the human condition had grown increasingly corrupt and that the monastics were indistinguishable from the vulgar commoners—greedy, gluttonous, and indolent, lacking any aspiration for the higher path. He therefore composed this "Exhortation" (Jingsai) to awaken them and urge them toward progress.
The commentary states: According to various sutras and śāstras, some titles are based on a single person, some on a single dharma, and others on both person and dharma combined.
This present *Jingsai* (Admonition) is titled precisely by way of both person and dharma; the two characters "Weishan" [refer to the person].

This was established by later generations and was not formulated by the Great Master himself. According to conventional commentarial practice, the author’s name is listed separately beneath the title;
however, since it is indicated here within the title itself, the work is named after both the person and the dharma.
Next, the explanation of the main text has two parts: first, the prose (long-phrase), and second, the verse (repeated stanza). △ First, the prose has two parts:
1. Instruction, and 2. Exposition of the Dharma. △ 1.
Instruction has nine parts: 1. The cause of karma and its fruit of suffering; 2. Birth, old age, death, and illness; 3. The time of arising and ceasing.

1. Urgency; 2. The four ways of transgressing secular norms to enter the Path; 3. How fame and profit cause one to lose the Path; 4. The instruction on the Three Studies; 5. The faults of failing to practice and study;
6. The ripening of karmic results in time; 7. Exhortation through encouragement to practice; 8.
The suffering of the fruit resulting from the cause of karma—since one’s body is bound by karma, one cannot escape the burden of physical form.
The first phrase clarifies karmic fruit; the second phrase clarifies manifold suffering (*saṃduḥkha*). This is the characteristic of suffering bound by karma.
Since karma belongs to the past and its fruit belongs to the present, it is said that there is bondage within the cause, and thus there is accumulation within the fruit.

Because this accumulation is not uniform, it is called "manifold suffering. As for "manifold suffering," briefly stated, there are the three sufferings and the eight sufferings; if explained extensively, there are eight [categories].
The fourteen thousand afflictions and various sufferings arise because ordinary beings do not understand their own minds; they give rise to delusions and create karma.
Bound by this karma, it is difficult to escape the physical burdens of the birth-and-death cycle of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*). As the Tiantai school says:
"All conditioned mental activities are constantly oppressed and distressed by the calamities of impermanence; therefore, they are called suffering. Wisdom [realizes this].
The Treatise states: "Immeasurable sentient beings have three kinds of physical suffering: old age, illness, and death; three kinds of mental suffering:
greed, hatred, and delusion; and three kinds of suffering in future lives: those of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. The *Dharmapada* states:
"In the past, there were four bhikṣus who discussed the sufferings of the world. One said that sexual desire torments people; another said that hunger and thirst oppress the body."
One word of anger causes turmoil; one word of alarm causes fear. You compete with one another over right and wrong. The Buddha said:
"What you are discussing does not investigate the meaning of suffering. The body is the root of all sufferings and the source of manifold afflictions.
You should seek quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*); this is the supreme bliss."
The commentary states: Now, the myriad burdens originate from the existence of a body; the body arises through the fetters of karma; and karma is acquired because of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because of the delusions of afflictions and ignorance (*avidyā*), one performs the karma of sentient beings. Due to this karma, sentient beings are bound and cannot attain liberation.
Consequently, within the three realms and six paths of existence, they undergo various forms and bodies. The multitude...
The burden of suffering: this arises because one receives a body due to karma, and the body, in turn, creates karma. To have a body is inevitably suffering; to have form is inevitably a burden.
Laozi also said: "I have a great affliction: it is that I have a mind. If I had no body, what affliction would there be?
To attain the state of no-body, one must first attain the state of no-mind. The mind functions as the instrument of karma, and karma arises from conditions.

If in a single thought-moment there is no arising, all afflictions and entanglements are simultaneously cast off. Thus, the *Zhao lun* states: "The proliferation of myriad entanglements is rooted in deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Once deluded conceptualization is dispelled, then the myriad entanglements are entirely stilled. Regarding the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*), they are: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and [the suffering of conditioned formations].

The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). This refers to sentient beings receiving the segmented body of the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), whose nature is constantly oppressive;
this is "suffering. Furthermore, when it is associated with painful sensation (*duḥkhā-vedanā*), it is suffering upon suffering, and is thus called "the suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

When a state of pleasure (*sukha-lakṣaṇa*) disintegrates, the characteristic of suffering immediately arises; this is called "the suffering of change" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). Contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are subject to the transition of the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
It flows and is perpetually unstable; therefore, it is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). As for the eight sufferings:

they are the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the intense accumulation of the five aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

This refers to the massing together of various sufferings such as birth, old age, sickness, and death; hence it is named the suffering of the intense accumulation of the five aggregates. This is termed "segmental" (*paricchinna*)...
Those who are Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas do not forget the marks of dharmas they grasp, and thus undergo the suffering of the transformation-death (pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa).
Ordinary beings, being shrouded by craving and views, fail to understand that objective realms are illusory; they give rise to delusions and create karma.

They undergo the suffering of分段生死 (paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa, segmented birth and death). As for what is called "afflictions" (kleśa), it refers to turbid and vexing dharmas that disturb and confuse the mind, creating vexation for the mind and causing the mind to suffer.
Briefly stated, these are the three poisons and the ten unwholesome actions;

extensively stated, they are the one hundred and eight afflictions, even up to the eighty-four thousand gates of *chen-lao* (dust-like toil). These gates of *chen-lao* are precisely the myriad entanglements.
Furthermore:
Second, birth, old age, sickness,
and death consist of the physical body inherited from one's parents, which is brought into being through the convergence of various conditions.

The first phrase clarifies the fundamental nature of form (*rūpa*); the second phrase clarifies its provisional aggregation. These two phrases together pertain to the phenomena of birth, which is the very source of all worldly burdens.
"Inheriting" (*bing*) means receiving by inheritance; "body" (*ti*) refers to the physical body composed of the four great elements.

From the very first moment of inverted thought, one gathers the impurities of the parents—the red and white elements—to constitute a body; hence it is called a "leftover body. To "rely on various conditions" (*jia zhong yuan*) means to rely on...

This refers to "borrowing," which is also synonymous with "relying upon. The various conditions consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "The four conditions combine through borrowing; thus, the six sense faculties falsely arise. The six sense faculties and the four great elements are synthesized from within and without."

Regarding the "four great elements," these are earth, water, fire, and wind. Their substances are each distinct; they lack any real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and possess no sovereign master capable of spontaneously combining them into a body.
They must necessarily be formed through three factors: past causes, various conditions, and the three [aspects of] action.
If causes and conditions are not complete, form does not abide. As for the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is said: because this exists, that exists.
With this arising, that arises: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form;

conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is becoming.
With birth as condition, there is aging and death; from these arise sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering accumulates and comes into being.
Now, these twelve factors are called "causes" because they successively induce their respective fruits;

they are called "conditions" because they exist by depending upon one another. When causes and conditions continue in succession, the cycle of birth and death proceeds without end. If [this process] is broken...
When ignorance does not give rise to grasping for existence, then the cycle of birth and death within the twenty-five states of existence across the three realms ceases entirely. That is to say:

because this is absent, that is absent; because this ceases, that ceases. From the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair—the entire accumulation of this great mass of suffering—all cease.

The Record states: "The body is formed by the temporary conjunction of various conditions (*pratyaya*). When conditions combine, it arises and is called birth; when conditions disperse, it ceases and is called death.
Therefore, because phenomena arise from conditions, they do not exist [independently]; because they arise through conditions, they are not non-existent.
Since they exist by virtue of conditions, there is no true sovereign or permanent master. *Zhi guan* says: "Examine each part—the head, feet, limbs, and joints—with meticulous observation."
One clearly perceives that there is no self; where, then, could there be a person or a sentient being?

The mechanism of karmic power is but a provisional empty village, arising from a multitude of conditions and lacking any sovereign master. The twelve links of dependent origination are also called "dependent arising" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) or "dependent birth.
This means that since the effect did not previously exist, its arising from those [conditions] is termed "cause. Fundamentally...
There are its constituent parts, which arise from that; these are called conditions (*pratyaya*). The first is called ignorance (*avidyā*), which carries the meaning of darkness and obscurity.
This refers to the delusions of affliction (*kleśa*) in past lives, which shroud the fundamental nature so that nothing is clearly understood.
The second is called formations (*saṃskāra*); "formations" refers to karmic actions. This refers to all wholesome and unwholesome deeds performed by body and speech in past lives.
This is karma. These two links are past causes. The third is consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness refers to the cognitive mind;

it means that, being drawn by the delusions and karma of the past, this consciousness enters and takes refuge in the mother’s womb. In a single kṣaṇa, with defiled craving as its seed, it receives the mental impression (*saṃjñā*) and forms the embryo.
It then gathers the two drops of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood, merging them into a single drop. Great!
It is like a bean seed abiding within the womb, in conjunction with three things: first, life; second, warmth; and third, consciousness.
Among these, the retributive wind that relies upon the [vital] wind is called "life-span. That the semen and blood do not become foul-smelling or putrid is called "warmth."
Among these, the mental faculty is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). These three factors must all be present; if even one is missing, they will decay and fail to endure.
This is the first seven-day stage of entry into the mother’s womb, termed the *kalala*, which resembles solidified butter.
From this point onward, following the mother’s inhalation and exhalation, it undergoes a transformation every seven days. As the *Zhiguan* states: "When a person is conceived in the womb..."
The spiritual consciousness first unites with the semen and blood; a cord remains at the navel, which is able to sustain and maintain it.
This is because the navel is the source of all the intestines and stomachs. While in the womb, the mother’s navel connects to the child’s navel;
thus, what the mother eats enters through the navel to nourish the child, and the same applies to the vital breaths. When the child first enters the womb, it relies upon—
Because it is the cessation of the mother’s breath, the worldly convention names the child "breath" (*āśvāsa*). Fourth is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*):
"name" refers to the mind, meaning that the mind exists only as a designation and lacks physical substance;

"form" refers to the physical body, meaning that from the time of entering the womb until the end of the fifth week, it is called the stage of formation, during which the various sense organs and limbs are produced and differentiated.

It is called "form" (*rūpa*). Taking the semen and blood of the parents as the seed of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) resides therein; therefore, these are combined and termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
Fifth is the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*). This refers to the period from after entering the womb until the sixth seventh-day interval, which is called the stage of hair, fur, nails, and teeth.
Upon reaching the seventh seventh-day interval, it is called the stage of possessing the faculties (*indriya-sampanna*), meaning that the six sense organs have opened.

"Zhang" (Expansion). It has the function of entering the six objects; therefore, it is called the "six entrances" (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The sixth is contact (*sparśa*). Contact means encountering or confronting.

This refers to the period from birth until the age of three or four, when the six faculties—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—though they encounter the six objects—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—are as yet unable to discern or experience the arising of suffering or pleasure.
Because it involves conceptualization, it is called "contact" (*sparśa*). The seventh is "feeling" (*vedanā*); "feeling" carries the meaning of experiencing or receiving.

This refers to the period from five or six years of age up to twelve or thirteen, when the six sense faculties encounter the six objects. At this stage, one is already able to receive and experience the qualities of the external objects, such as their being pleasant or unpleasant;
although one can distinguish them, one has not yet given rise to a mind of craving, attachment, or sexual defilement. These are the five factors.
This is the present fruit. The eighth is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving is precisely greedy craving;
it refers to the period from ages fourteen or fifteen up to eighteen or nineteen, when one craves various excellent and wonderful requisites, as well as objects such as sexual desire.

However, because one is not yet able to pursue these extensively and universally, it is called craving. The ninth is grasping (*upādāna*). Grasping is precisely seeking and seizing; it refers to [the period] from age twenty...
After the age of ten, craving increases further; one runs about in all four directions, seeking the five sensory objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
Therefore, this is called "clinging" (*upādāna*). The tenth is "existence" (*bhava*); existence refers to future existence, for the continuity of cause and effect does not perish.

This refers to how, by seeking and grasping at various objects, one gives rise to wholesome and unwholesome karma, which accumulates and draws forth the fruits of the three realms of existence—the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
These three links constitute the present causes. The eleventh is birth (*jāti*), which means taking rebirth;
it refers to the wholesome and unwholesome karma performed in this life that leads to rebirth in the three realms in a future life.

This refers to taking birth within the six realms of existence. The twelfth is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). "Old age" means the maturation of the faculties; "death" means the destruction of the faculties.

That is to say, after having taken birth in a future life, the reaching of the maturation of the body consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is called old age; once matured, its subsequent disintegration is called death.
These two links are the fruits of the future. These twelve links constitute the law of cause and effect across the three periods of time, circulating without interruption.

Because ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of the past serve as causes, they evoke these present factors—consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—as their fruits.
Due to these fruits, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) arise, constituting the present.
This is the cause. By virtue of this cause, one brings about the fruit of birth, old age, and death in future lives.

The fruit, in turn, creates further causes, and those causes again bring about fruits; thus, the three periods of time continue in succession without interruption, like the turning of a wheel. Therefore, it is called *saṃsāra* (the cycle of rebirth).
Although the four great elements support one another, they are constantly in opposition.
The first phrase refers to their provisional combination; the second phrase refers to their discordant nature.

When a person gathers the external earth, water, fire, and wind to form a body, they mutually assist and sustain one another, upholding the life-faculty and remaining for the duration of a single lifetime. Yet, within this process, they are constantly...
When they are discordant, there is a great lack of harmony, and one hundred and one diseases arise.
When the four great elements are out of balance, then four hundred and four diseases manifest simultaneously. As for what is called "great," it refers to these four dharmas;

because they exist nowhere that they are not present and pervade all regions, they are termed "great. All things and all forms are composed of these four great elements; externally, they constitute earth and wood.
Mountains and rivers, when within, constitute the four limbs and hundred bones; they coalesce to form life and disperse to form death.
In life they are internal; in death they are external. Although the internal and external differ, their fundamental nature is no different. Their solid quality belongs to earth.
These include the hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, and so forth; if these were not dependent upon water, they would not cohere.
Moisture is the property of water. This also includes mucus, saliva, semen, and the excretions of both large and small intestines; if these were not dependent upon earth, [they would not exist].
It would then simply flow away and dissipate. The nature of heat belongs to fire; it is the warmth within the body.

If it were not assisted by wind, it would not increase. The nature of motion belongs to wind; it is the inhalation and exhalation, as well as the movement and turning of the body. If this wind were absent, [it would not function].
Consequently, the body is unable to move or perform actions. However, these four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are by nature originally free from affliction;
it is through the gathering of various conditions that they increase, decrease, or mutually overcome one another, whereby illness arises. Thus, when earth increases, the body becomes heavy;
when water accumulates, mucus and saliva become abnormal; when fire blazes, the head and chest suffer from intense heat; and when wind moves, the vital breath...
The afflictions of respiratory distress, heaviness, phlegm, jaundice, and the arising of wind-humors—through these four types of diseases, the four hundred and four diseases arise.
There are one hundred and one wind-diseases, one hundred and one bile-diseases, one hundred and one phlegm-diseases, and one hundred and one combined-diseases.
Such ailments arise at all times; therefore, they are said to be "constantly present."
Contradiction.

The Record states: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says, "The four great elements constitute the body, and they constantly afflict one another. Within each of the four great elements, one hundred and one diseases arise.
Because of the arising of water and wind, there are two hundred and two cold diseases. Because of the earth [element], there are two hundred and two hot diseases."

Because fire arises, it has the characteristic of heat; earth has the characteristic of solidity. Because of its solid nature, it is difficult to digest; because it is difficult to digest, it can give rise to febrile diseases.
Blood, flesh, sinews, bones, vessels, marrow, and so forth are the constituents of earth.

Excluding those [factors] resulting from karmic retribution, all phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "When the four great elements are in disharmony, one suffers from physical labor and toil."
There is no fixed time [for its onset]. One is forced to carry heavy loads and is buffeted by cold and heat. When external heat assists fire, the fire becomes powerful and breaks the water;

this is the increase of the fire-disease (*tejo-roga*). When external cold assists water, the water increases and harms the fire; this is the water-disease (*āpo-roga*). External wind moves the vital breath (*vāyu*).

When the vital energy (vāyu) blows upon the fire, the fire moves the water; this constitutes a wind disorder (*vāta-vyādhi*). Alternatively, when the three great elements increase and afflict the earth element, it is called a disorder of equal proportions (*sāma-bhāga-vyādhi*).
Or, when the constituent parts of the body increase and afflict the three great elements, this is likewise a disorder of equal proportions belonging to the earth element.

Furthermore, immoderation in food and drink can also produce illness: for instance, pungent substances such as ginger and cinnamon increase the fire element, while sugarcane and honey—sweet and cold—increase the water element.
Pears increase wind; oily fats increase earth; and cucumbers serve as the causal conditions for heat-related illnesses.
This is what is meant by consuming food that is unsuitable, thereby giving rise to disease. As the ancients said: "Illness enters through the mouth; calamity issues from the mouth.
This is precisely what that refers to.
Impermanence, old age, and sickness do not make appointments with people.
The first phrase clarifies the three marks; the second phrase clarifies the absence of a master. The three marks are fundamentally empty, and originally there is no self.

How could they act as a master to arbitrarily set a date for their arrival? Only those who eliminate their discriminative consciousness and realize the fundamental source can do so; the ignorant cannot.
This is non-awakening. "Impermanence" means that what was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed for a brief moment, returns to non-existence;
it refers to that which does not abide for even a single *kṣaṇa*. From the time of emerging from the womb, through youth, to old age, to sickness, and finally until the end of life.
In the interim, moments of consciousness shift and flow without ceasing; therefore, it is called "impermanence" (*anitya*), which is also another name for death.

"Old age" refers to the state where the faculties have ripened and declined, the physical form is withered and the complexion is haggard, the spirit is dim and obscured, the hair is white, and the face is wrinkled—meaning that death will not be long in coming.
"Sickness" refers to the disharmony of the four great elements, the arising of the four hundred [diseases], and the exhaustion of physical strength.
One suffers defeat; food and drink become unpalatable; the spirit is diminished; and one requires assistance to sit or rise. For these reasons, it is called "sickness.
If one considers the sequence of dharmas as they arise in succession, then death follows later. However, now, by means of the single dharma of impermanence, its essence pervades all things.
This is because all phenomena are subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The Record states: "Moment by moment they do not abide; thought after thought they do not remain; this is called impermanence. A sutra says: "The power of impermanence is great;
its swiftness exceeds that of flowing water or mountains. The *Zhēlùn* (Treatise on Refutation) states: "There are three kinds of impermanence: first, destruction moment by moment (*kṣaṇabhanga*)."
1. The impermanence of cessation; 2. The impermanence of the separation of combinations; 3. The ultimate impermanence of suchness. Regarding the first three:
at the time of birth and death, life is swift—surviving in the morning and perishing by evening; in a single *kṣaṇa*, one passes into another world.
The first phrase refers to the present life; the second phrase refers to future lives. These two phrases together explain the meaning of impermanence (*anitya*).
Below, this is further clarified through metaphors such as frost and dew. Regarding the term "kṣaṇa" (moment): it denotes the utmost brevity of time.
This means that when a person approaches death and relinquishes their lifespan, it occurs in a mere single final *kṣaṇa*; at that very instant, the sense faculties perish and consciousness departs.
"Ji" (the limit) refers to the moment when one abandons this current body and receives another physical form. "Consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness;

departing, it lingers at the rear, while arriving, it acts as the vanguard. In a single kṣaṇa, it seizes the semen and blood of the parents and dwells within the womb, becoming the root of birth and death and the source of the fruit of suffering.
The record states: There are eight kinds of consciousness: first, visual consciousness; second, auditory consciousness; third, olfactory consciousness; fourth, gustatory consciousness;
fifth, tactile consciousness; sixth, mental consciousness; seventh, the manas consciousness; and eighth, the ālaya-vijñāna.
It is like spring frost or morning dew; in an instant, they vanish.

The first phrase establishes the substance (*tī*), and the second phrase explains its nature (*svabhāva*). Since frost and dew dissolve upon meeting the sun, their substance is not solid and their nature is not permanent.
"Like" (*pī-yǔ*) is a term used to establish a simile; "in an instant" (*shū-hù*) means existing for a brief moment before ceasing to be.
The commentary states: These two phrases of the main text explain the phrase "morning existence and evening death," collectively clarifying the swiftness of time.
"Sū" (倐) means rapidity. The *Zongjing* says: "Though one may live for a hundred years, it is still like a single kṣaṇa;
like a long wave rushing eastward, like the fading light of the setting sun, like sparks struck from stone, or like a swift horse galloping through a crack."
A tiny lamp in the wind, morning dew upon the tips of grass, a withered tree at the edge of a precipice, or a flash of lightning that dazzles the eyes—
were one not to encounter the True Dharma, one would surely fall forever into the dark paths of suffering.
"A tree on the bank and a vine in a well—how could these endure for long?
The first phrase establishes the essential nature (*tattva*), while the second phrase explains its meaning. A tree standing on a precipice cannot be long-lasting;
how can a vine invaded by two rats endure? The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a man who, to avoid two intoxicated elephants, climbed a vine and entered a well. Below..."
Three dragons spat fire and bared their claws; he immediately suspended himself from a vine. Above, two rats—one black and one white—gnawed at the vine, which was on the verge of snapping.
Beside him, four snakes sought to sting him. As the man looked upward, two elephants had already arrived at the edge of the well.
In his distress and lack of refuge, a bee suddenly passed by and left five drops of honey that fell into his mouth. As the man tasted the honey, he completely forgot his peril and fear.

Now, two intoxicated elephants are used as a metaphor for birth and death; the creeping vine represents the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); entering the well represents impermanence (*anityatā*); the two rats represent the sun and moon;

the four snakes represent the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); the three dragons represent the three poisons (*trivisa*); and the five drops of honey [represent the fleeting pleasures of existence].
This is a metaphor for the five desires. The three poisons are the cause of the three evil realms; therefore, if even one of the vines is severed, there is immediately the danger of falling.
The Record states:
"The two phrases of the original text explain the single phrase 'not meeting with others at an appointed time. This clarifies that months, days, and years pass swiftly."
Furthermore, the body is like a tree on a precipice; once the winds of karma arrive, no strength can pull it back. Life is like a vine in a well;
as the days and months gradually diminish, they cause people not to realize that the tree by the cliff does not grow year after year, nor that the vine in the well is aging so rapidly.
Regarding the "vine in the well," this refers to a vine growing at the edge of a well; some say it refers to the roots of a tree. "Well" (井) refers to—
"Qiuqu" refers to a desolate mound and a dried-up well. Dharma Master Kumārajīva said: "In the past, there was a criminal who, fearing his punishment, fled.
The king ordered a drunken elephant to pursue him. In his desperate terror, the man threw himself into a dried-up well," and so forth.
The "three poisons" are greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*). The "three evil realms" are hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. The "five desires" are form and sound... [and so on].
These are fragrance, flavor, and touch. Alternatively, wealth, form, fame, food, and sleep are taken as the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).
It is said that sentient beings, deluded by these five desires and attached to their minor pleasures, completely forget the perilous sufferings of birth and death.
"Each thought-moment is swift.
"Thought" (*smṛti*) refers to the deluded thoughts of the arising and ceasing of the mind in ordinary beings. Before the preceding thought has ceased, the succeeding thought arises;
thus, each thought-moment arises and ceases, like a lamp burning its wick, arising and ceasing without pause. Such is the characteristic of the swiftness of this arising and ceasing.
Those who do not possess the eye of wisdom cannot see this.

The commentary states: "This clarifies the swiftness of thought. Because they are deluded thoughts, they arise and perish without ceasing; the true mind, however, is eternally abiding and does not shift."
In a single *kṣaṇa*, a breath may turn and one is already in the next life.
The Sanskrit term *kṣaṇa* here refers to a "single thought-moment" (*ekacitta-ksana*), which is the most rapid unit of time.

The *Saṃghīti-sūtra* states that twenty *nimeṣas* (thought-moments) constitute one *tatkṣaṇa* (instant), and twenty *tatkṣaṇas* are called one finger-snap (*acchaṭā*). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that it is the duration of a strong man snapping his fingers once.
Recently, it has been established that there are sixty-five *kṣaṇas* [in one thought-moment]. However, thoughts have both large and small durations.

As for the "large thought," there are ninety *kṣaṇas* within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), and within each *kṣaṇa*, there are nine hundred instances of arising and ceasing. This is what is meant by "one *kṣaṇa*."
"Minor mindfulness" refers to the breath, which is the inhalation and exhalation. This breath is called "life-span" (*āyus*);

it is termed "span" (*āyu*) because it lasts for one period [of existence], and it is termed "life" (*jīvita*) because it maintains continuity. Since the wind of the breath is maintained continuously throughout this single period without interruption, the inhalation and exhalation are called "life-span.
When it turns—that is, once it has gone out and does not enter again—it is called "the end of life. This occurs in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
"Interval" refers to the moment when the eighth consciousness relinquishes the preceding aggregate and receives the succeeding aggregate.

The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not explicitly mentioned here because by citing the preceding and succeeding states, the interval between them is inherently included. Furthermore, the duration of the intermediate state is indeterminate:

it may last for seven weeks at the longest, or as briefly as a single thought-moment; having thus relinquished the intermediate state, one immediately receives the subsequent existence. This refers generally to those who come to be born in a future life.
These six realms are places where one is reborn as a retribution for good or evil karma.
The Record states: "The two phrases of the main text explain the preceding phrase 'different worlds in a single kṣaṇa.

This clarifies the swiftness of a *kṣaṇa*. Superior goodness leads to birth in the heavens; middling goodness leads to birth among humans; inferior goodness leads to birth as an asura. Superior evil leads to..."
Those of middling evil are born as hungry ghosts; those of inferior evil are born as animals. "To blink" refers to the movement of the eyes.

Regarding the "intermediate state" (antarābhava): when a person's life ends and the inhalation and exhalation cease, the eighth consciousness abandons the previous physical body, and immediately there exists an intermediate body in the midst of space, invisible and dark, which takes fragrance as food. In this...
There is a place where conditions meet; there, one sees one's parents in union. The light of the fire of desire arrives as soon as it is thought of.
Through inverted perception, in a single kṣaṇa, one seizes the two drops—red and white—and forms the subsequent aggregates (paścādbhava-skandha).

At that moment, the intermediate state (antarābhava) body ceases. If the place of birth has not yet been determined, or if the parents do not unite, this intermediate state body remains for seven days.
From the first death until the seventh seven-day period, one will certainly take rebirth; it does not exceed forty-nine days.

If that karmic retribution is already fixed, whether one is born among humans or devas, or falls into the realms of ghosts or animals, in a single kṣaṇa one discards the previous aggregate (pūrvātmabhāva) to receive the intermediate state (antarābhava), and discarding the intermediate state, receives the subsequent aggregate.
This is swifter than a flash of lightning and cannot be measured by ordinary beings; only a Buddha [can know it].
"One is able to know.
Why then do you remain so complacent and let time pass in vain?
Why do you still act as you do? These are also words of cross-examination, as well as expressions that take up what precedes and turn toward what follows. Based on the above...
This demonstrates the knowledge that the faults and afflictions of birth and death are impermanent and swift.

It intends to lead those below to awaken to the truth of renouncing the mundane world to enter the Path, practicing diligently according to the Dharma with the hope of escaping saṃsāra. "Yanran" means peace and ease; it refers in general to the rapid passage of time.

Human life is impermanent. Why do you eat your fill all day long, letting your mind remain idle, thus passing your time in complacent emptiness, without devising means for spiritual advancement to escape birth and death?
4. Contradicting worldly norms to enter the Way:
one’s parents no longer receive succulent delicacies, and the six types of relatives are firmly abandoned and separated.
The former phrase lacks the repayment of nourishment; the latter phrase lacks respectful harmony. Parents are the heaven and earth of their children. As the *Shijing* says: [text missing]
It is said: "Alas, alas! Our parents gave us life through their toil. To repay their kindness, it would be as vast as the great heavens and beyond measure.
A sutra states: "If one makes offerings to one's parents, one obtains immeasurable merit. The Buddha said: "Parents provide great benefit to their children;
they nourish them with milk and nurture them according to the seasons until the four elements of the body are formed. If a person were to carry their father on their right shoulder..."
Carrying his mother on his left shoulder for a hundred years, he relieved himself upon her back without ever harboring a heart of resentment.
He provided her with the four requisites of life without fail; yet, even such a son cannot fully repay the kindness of his parents.

One who wishes to repay their kindness should exhort their parents toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and toward the principles of cause and effect: leading those who have not yet developed faith to believe, and leading those who already believe to...
To cause [virtue] to increase; to exhort those who lack pure precepts to receive and uphold them; to exhort those with stinginess and greed to practice giving;

and to exhort those who lack superior wisdom to cultivate it, thereby causing them to dwell securely in goodness and achieve self-subduing—this is what is called truly repaying the kindness of one's parents.
"The six relations" refers to father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, and children. It is also said: "One father."
1. One's own two sons; 2. paternal uncles; 3. paternal first cousins; 4. paternal second cousins; 5. paternal third cousins; 6. clan cousins.
Regarding "abandoning and leaving": the Sūtra states that when a Bodhisattva leaves the household life, they abandon these six types of relatives, neither recording nor recollecting them.
One must diligently cultivate the path of practice in order to swiftly achieve Bodhi.
The commentary states: "Delicious food" refers to fine cuisine.

That even this is insufficient to repay the kindness of one's parents means that although one may provide for them with physical care and never disobey their wishes, one cannot thereby place their spirits in the higher realms; rather, one seeks to benefit their souls through many lifetimes.
Such a person must be encouraged to observe the fasts and precepts and extensively cultivate merit and wisdom.

If they are one who has left the household life, and their parents are impoverished and unable to support themselves, the Buddha permitted them to teach those parents with faith, bestow upon them the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and thereafter seek alms to provide for them.
Master Nanshan said: "A true renunciant fears the manifold sufferings of the four enemies and detests the three realms."
The impermanence of all things. To renounce the deepest affection for one's six kin and abandon profound attachment to the five desires—one who can do so is called a true renunciant.
Such a person may then cause the Three Jewels to flourish and deliver beings from the four modes of birth; the benefit is most profound, and their merit is immeasurable.
They cannot stabilize the state or govern the realm; their family estates are suddenly abandoned, and their lineage is severed.
The first line lacks [the phrase] "to assist the sovereign and benefit the people"; the second line lacks [the phrase] "to inherit the estate and continue the lineage.

When a śramaṇa leaves the household life, he renounces procreation and the continuation of his lineage to propagate and glorify the seed of the Triple Gem. Although this may appear to lack loyalty and filial piety, in establishing one's person...

They practice the Way to repay the kindness of their parents and preach the Dharma to encourage virtue, thereby transforming others through the teachings of the Celestial Sovereign. To repay such benevolence in this manner—what could possibly surpass it?
Formerly, Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty said to He Shangzhi: "If all within the realm were to follow the pure teachings of Śākyamuni..."
"Then I shall sit and bring about the Great Peace. Shangzhi replied:

"In a village of a hundred households, if ten people observe the five precepts, those ten will become pure and prudent. In a town of a thousand houses, if a hundred people cultivate the ten wholesome deeds, those hundred will be harmonious and friendly.
If a person can practice one good deed, they eliminate one evil; if one evil is eliminated, one punishment ceases."

Punishment ceases within the family; when ten thousand punishments cease, they cease within the state. This is what is meant by the "clear intent" [of the sages] regarding the attainment of Great Peace through stillness.
The Records say: "When those above clarify their conduct, they diverge from worldly custom; when those below clarify their conduct, they enter the Way."
"Far removed from one's hometown and kin; shaving the head and receiving instruction from a teacher.

The first phrase refers to leaving the secular world, and the second phrase refers to entering the Way. "Far removed" (*mian*) means distance; it signifies being distanced from local customs and inclining toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is precisely abandoning the household to proceed toward the homeless life. "Shaving the head and receiving instruction from a teacher" means discarding the outward appearance and deportment of the laity.
To discard worldly finery and emulate the Tathāgata, to be endowed with the marks and virtues of a Buddha, and to receive instruction from a teacher and learn under them—
this is the profound rule for entering the Way and the grand paradigm for transcending the world.

The commentary states: In the world, facial hair and long locks are considered ornaments of one’s appearance and objects of aesthetic preference. When a bhikṣu leaves the household life, he opposes worldly custom to pursue the Way;

he discards what the world prizes and severs all attachments to affection. To now retain facial hair and long locks while calling oneself a *dhūta* is for the name to be in rebellion against the practice and the conduct to be at variance with the name.
The Sanskrit term *dhūta* translates here as "shaking off" (*dǒusǒu*), meaning to shake off the three [poisons].

Regarding the realms, worldly dust, and afflictions, their practice consists of twelve dharmas. To now claim that one who has disheveled hair is called a *dhūta* is an extreme perversion and falsehood.
The Buddha said: "Long beard, hair, and nails are the marks of an evil bhikṣu who has broken the precepts.
However, for a forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣu living alone who has no one to shave him, it is permitted for his hair to grow to a maximum length of one [finger-width]."
An inch. A fingernail should be no longer than a single grain of barley; it must not exceed that.
"One who leaves home for the homeless life" means one who abandons the worldly household and enters the dwelling of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Why does the Tathāgata say that the kindness of parents is great and must not go unrequited? Furthermore, he says that the kindness of teachers and preceptors cannot be measured. Its...
"Who is the greatest? The Buddha said: "As for those who remain at home, they serve their parents with filial piety while remaining in their lap;

because the debt of gratitude for their upbringing cannot be repaid, and because the kindness of giving birth and raising them is profound, they are said to be 'great. If one follows a teacher to study and develop insight and knowledge, that kindness is next in greatness.
Now, as for those who leave the household life, they abandon the house of their parents—the realm of birth and death."
To enter into the Dharma-gate and receive the subtle and wondrous Dharma is due to the power of the Teacher.

To cause the Dharma-body to grow, to produce the wealth of merit, and to nourish the life of wisdom—no achievement is greater than this. To follow those who gave birth [to one's physical body] is merely secondary.
As for "xiāngdǎng" (鄉黨), "xiāng" means "orientation," referring to that which all people turn toward; "dǎng" means "faction" or "party. In antiquity, it was used for groups of five hundred.
A household constitutes a *dang* (party). The *Rites of Zhou* states: "Within one hundred households is called a *xiang* (district).

The *Han Annals* defines five households as a *lin* (neighborhood), five *lin* as a *li* (village), four *li* as a *zu* (clan), five *zu* as a *dang*, five *dang* as a *zhou* (prefecture), and five *zhou* as a *xiang*.
Thus, it is by means of twelve thousand five hundred households that a *xiang* is formed. *Bing* (to receive) means to accept a mandate.
Within, one diligently exerts the power of mindful reflection; without, one widely propagates the virtue of non-contention.
The former phrase clarifies mindfulness and wisdom; the latter phrase clarifies harmony and respect.

To apply mindfulness and wisdom within and to expound the six points of harmony without constitutes the merit of entering the Way and the foundation for establishing virtue. Master Zhao said: "Without a true mind, there is nothing [to rely upon]."
One must possess six qualities. Without these six qualities, one cannot harmonize the community. If the community is not harmonious, it is not the foundation of respect and obedience.

The Record states: First, harmony of precepts through collective practice; second, harmony of views through shared understanding; third, harmony of body through dwelling together; fourth, harmony of benefit...
Harmony and concord. Fifth, harmony in speech means being free from contention. Sixth, harmony in intention means being uniformly joyful and utterly detached from the mundane world.
One hopes for and aspires toward liberation.

The former phrase refers to leaving the household of worldly society; the latter phrase refers to leaving the household of the three realms. To escape the secular dust of the world, one must first set foot upon the path.
"Transcending the mundane world; aspiring to transcend the three realms and severing the afflictions—this finally accords with the fundamental vow of leaving the household life.
These two sentences summarize the preceding text and introduce the following discourse.
The commentary states: "The first phrase summarizes the five points concerning parents, the six types of relatives, the state, the succession of heirs, and the local community;

the second phrase summarizes the three points concerning shaving the head, diligent internal practice, and broad external propagation. *Jiong* (逈) means remote and vast. *Ji* (冀) means desire or hope. *Wang* (望) also means to look toward with expectation.
5. Regarding the loss of the Way through seeking fame and profit:
how is it that as soon as one has ascended to the level of the precepts, one immediately declares, "I am a bhikṣu"?

The first phrase clarifies that there is no actual practice at the very moment one receives the precepts; the second phrase clarifies that the virtue of cessation (*śīla*) is not yet complete. This is because one's reputation does not accord with one's conduct.

This does not accord with the meaning of the term "bhikṣu. Having left one's kin to enter the Way, striving within and propagating without, the original purpose was to bring an end to birth and death.

Why, as soon as you have entered the ranks of the Saṃgha, do you immediately greedily crave fame and profit, becoming dissolute and indulgent in your passions, creating causes for outflows and binding yourself to the fruits of saṃsāra?
Thus, you contradict your initial resolve and lose the practice of liberation. This occurs as soon as you ascend to the level of the precepts.
This refers to the initial accomplishment of the unconditioned (*avijñapti*) through the formal reception of the complete precepts. There are four categories of precepts:

namely, the five precepts, the ten precepts, the complete precepts (*upasampadā*), and the bodhisattva precepts. The first and last of these apply to both lay and monastic practitioners; the middle two apply exclusively to monastics.
As for the statement "I am a bhikṣu," this refers to one who possesses the complete precepts. *Bhikṣu* is a Sanskrit term whose name contains three meanings.
Regarding the meaning: first, destroying evil; second, terrifying Māra; third, the mendicant. Because it contains these three meanings, it cannot be translated;
therefore, the original sound is retained. The record states:
that which has no creator is also called "non-instruction" (avijñapti) and is further named "non-manifest form" (avijñapti-rūpa); this is the essence of the precepts (*śīla*). From...
It is obtained through three *karmas*. Once this substance has been attained, one spontaneously ceases evil and spontaneously practices good;
there is no need for further effort, and thus it is called "non-action" (*avijñapti*). As for the term "cessation," it means to stop and sever all evils so that they do not arise again.

"Destroying evil" means that, as when first receiving the precepts, one generates the wholesome discipline (*kuśala-saṃvara*) through the three *karmavācanās*, thereby destroying the unwholesome discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*).
If one considers this in terms of both practice and understanding, it can destroy the evils of the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought (*saṃjñā-kleśa*).
"Frightening Māra" means that, having already destroyed evil, the King Māra thinks: "This person will not only leave my realm, but may even transmit the lamp [of the Dharma] and transform others."

"My retinue is gone; my palace is empty; therefore, I have become terrified. Regarding the term "beggar" (*bhikṣu*): "beggar" (*bhikṣu*) is a name for one who begs or seeks, while "gentleman" (*sū*) is a title for one who is refined and pure.
This means that internally he cultivates refined and pure virtue, and externally he abstains from the four types of improper food.
Dwelling in a pure livelihood, he brings benefit and merit to sentient beings, shatters the mind of arrogance, and remains humble and self-effacing. Thus he spoke.
One seeks the requisites for sustaining the body in order to accomplish the virtue of refined purity. Nowadays, many people seek much and store much;
how can this be called the virtue of refined purity? Since one has already deviated from its name, can such a person still be considered a bhikṣu?
Regarding "that which the donor requires for consumption belongs to the permanent endowment" (*sādhāraṇa-vastu*):

the first phrase clarifies the gift of faith, while the second phrase clarifies the property of the Sangha. If one lacks the virtue of the precepts, then not even a single thread or a drop of water can be digested;
how much more so the four types of offerings from a donor or the enjoyments of the *saṃghika* (Sangha) property? As for "the donor" (*dānapati*): *dāna* is...

"Xīyīn" (西音) means "giving" (*dāna*) here. "Yuè" (越) is a term from this region [of China] meaning that one who is able to practice giving will, life after life, transcend the ocean of suffering of poverty.
There are four types of permanent property (*āvenika-dharmya*): first, permanent property that is permanently fixed.

This refers to monastic dwellings, communal utensils, flowers, fruits, fields, gardens, servants, livestock, and so forth. Because their substance is restricted to a specific location, they do not extend to other realms.
It may only be used for consumption and is not permitted to be divided or sold; therefore, it is specifically termed "permanent property" (*sthavira-vastu*).

Second, "universal permanent property" refers to, for example, the regular meals provided for the monastics within a monastery. Its substance extends to all ten directions, yet its application is restricted to the specific location. These two are called *saṃghika* (monastic) property.
Third, "present before" (*pratyutpanna*) refers to property currently received as a gift by the monastic community; it is bestowed solely upon those present at this particular place.
Because it belongs to the *saṃgha*, it is present before the four directions. It is like the light property of the five groups of renunciants who have passed away.

If the *karman* has not yet been performed, the object belongs to the *saṃgha* of the ten directions; if the *karman* has already been performed, the object belongs to the *saṃgha* present before one's eyes. These two are called "objects belonging to the *saṃgha* present before one's eyes."
The Record states: "What is required" refers generally to items for consumption and use; "what is used for eating" is restricted to food and drink;
"what is used for medicine" extends to clothing, bedding, dwellings, and so forth.
They do not understand or reflect upon the origin [of these phenomena], claiming instead that it is "the natural law (dharmatā) for them to be provided.
The former phrase loses its contemplation, while the latter is a deluded deliberation. Because they lack the wisdom of contemplation, they do not understand or reflect upon the Dharma.
Due to the darkness of delusion, they give rise to separate ignorant views; from this, shamelessness, lack of remorse, arrogance, indolence, greed, and envy arise.
"Reflecting" (*vitarka*) means deliberation; "thinking" (*vicāra*) means weighing. "Speaking" refers to utterances that are not mere idle chatter.
"Natural law" (*dharmatā*) refers to what is inherently appropriate according to principle. There are two kinds of "proper offerings": first, others deem it appropriate to make offerings to oneself;
second, one deems it appropriate to receive offerings from others. Regarding the "place of origin," this refers to calculating the amount of rice in a single bowl. As for the "agent":

The merit involved is no small matter. A donor sacrifices their own share for wife and children to plant seeds in the field of merit; yet if one’s own virtue is incomplete, how could it be appropriate to receive such offerings?
Even if one is endowed with all virtues, one must still engage in contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) to properly digest the offerings of the faithful.
Thus, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva lacks contemplation, they should not even eat food."
The Record states: The *Kāśyapa Sūtra* says that at that time, five hundred bhikṣus said, "We are unable to practice with diligence;
we fear we cannot digest the offerings of the faithful. We beg to return to lay life.

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva praised them, saying, "If you cannot digest the food of the faithful's offerings, it would be better to return to lay life hundreds of times in a single day than to break [the precepts] even once in a day."

Regarding the precept on receiving the faithful offerings of others, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "If there are those who practice dhyāna and attain liberation, I permit them to receive the food offered by the faithful.
Master Cien (Cimin) said: "One wears no silk and eats no grain from the fields.

The sweat and blood of weavers and plowmen are offered so that the work of the Path may be accomplished. If the work of the Path has not yet been accomplished, how can one possibly digest [such offerings]?"—Compassionate Reception.

Master Shen said: "Nowadays, there are some beginners who, having eaten their fill and slept soundly, pass their days according to their own whims and yet still complain that it does not meet their expectations.
They do not realize that an ordained person is like a whetstone.
When anyone needs a sharp blade, they come to the stone to grind it. As others' blades become sharp through this constant grinding, the stone itself gradually wears away."
To diminish and thin [the afflictions]. Some even resent that others do not come to grind [their nails] upon their stones; what great benefit is there in this?

These words are most poignant, like applying a golden needle to the seat of a person’s illness. Even if one were to possess a stone as hard as diamond, it would still not prevent one from resenting that others do not come to grind upon it.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Reflect upon this food: it was produced through plowing, planting, weeding, and harvesting..."

It is harvested, threshed, and treated; it is pounded, ground, sifted, and boiled before it is finally prepared. The labor required is immense. Calculating for even a single bowl of rice, it is produced through the accumulated sweat of laborers.
The food consumed is small, while the sweat shed is great; such is the heavy toil and hardship involved in its production.
Yet, once it enters the mouth and is eaten, it immediately becomes impure and possesses no further value. Thus, what was once [fresh] from the previous day...
In an instant, it turns into excrement and urine. What was originally a delicious flavor, which people relish, becomes impure—something foul that one does not wish to behold.
The practitioner should reflect upon such wretched food: "If I become greedily attached to this, I shall fall into hell and eat glowing iron balls;
when I emerge from hell, I shall fall among the animals, such as oxen, sheep, or camels, to repay my debt."

Regarding past debts: one may be reborn as a pig or a dog, constantly devouring filth and excrement. Contemplating it in this way, one should give rise to a sense of weary detachment before being fit to receive food.
Master Dao’an said: "The gravity of the reduction [of karmic weight] is such that for every grain of rice, there are seven pounds [of suffering].

One who eats offerings without the precepts will, after death, enter Mount Tai; they shall have burning iron for food and molten copper poured down their throats. Such is the agony described in the *Dharmapada*.
As for what has been stated: those who study the Way but do not penetrate its principle return the offerings of the faithful with their own bodies;

such people are eighty-one in number, and for them, the tree shall not grow. However, if one turns the light of the mind back for even a single thought-moment and suddenly merges with the Way, even ten thousand taels of gold can be consumed.
Having finished eating, they gather together in a noisy clamor, speaking only of various worldly matters.

The first phrase provides a general heading; the second phrase offers a specific explanation. Since it was not yet clear what was being said in the "noisy clamor," it is explained as "various worldly matters.
"Having finished eating" means having eaten one's fill. "Gather together" means to assemble in a group. "Various matters" refers to miscellaneous talk.
These are merely worldly words that do not pertain to the discourse of the Sūtras and Vinaya.

If one lacks the mindfulness of self-mastery, and if the speech uttered externally is improper, and if one does not cultivate meditative insight (*vipaśyanā*), how can one understand through reflection? If the three karmas are not diligently restrained, agitation (*auddhatya*) will arise.

As the *Śāsana-parivarta Sūtra* states: "If there are various frivolous discourses (*prapañca*), the mind becomes distracted; even though one has left the household life, one is still not liberated. This is so.
Therefore, one must urgently abandon the mind of frivolous proliferation and distraction, and seek the bliss of unconditioned quiescence (*asaṃskṛta-nirvāṇa*).
Those who wish to attain the bliss of quiescence should solely and skillfully restrain their minds and eliminate the affliction of frivolous proliferation.
As Chan Master Changlu Ze’s *Self-Admonition* states: "If one were to surreptitiously discuss the affairs of the imperial court or privately critique the administration of a commandery..."
In the offices of the local magistrates, they discussed the abundance or scarcity of the realm’s resources and debated the excellence or depravity of local customs.
This extended even to the minor affairs of commerce and industry, the idle talk of the marketplace, military conflicts on the frontiers, and banditry in the Central Plains.

Regarding literature, arts, clothing, food, and wealth, they relied upon their own strengths while concealing the virtues of others; they exaggerated manifest faults and pointed out the slightest flaws.
Since this deviates from meritorious deeds, it offers no benefit to the mind set on the Way. Such idle talk alike harms true virtue;

one consumes the offerings of the faithful in vain and looks upward with shame before the dragons and devas. The sin begins as a mere trickle, yet the calamity ends with the destruction of one's very head. Why is this?

While the fires of suffering for sentient beings burn from all four sides, how can one sit at ease discussing what is meaningless? Even the ancient masters spoke thus to admonish themselves; I— [am no different].
Who among these people would not fail to reflect upon themselves?
The record states: "Xuan" means clamor. Regarding "restlessness" (*auddhatya*), there are three types:

first, restlessness of body, which refers to a fondness for wandering about, various playful antics, and an inability to remain seated even for a moment; second, restlessness of speech, which refers to a fondness for chanting and competing [in recitation].
These are non-beneficial frivolous discourses (*prapañca*) and worldly talk, among other such things.

Third is mental agitation (*auddhatya*), which refers to the mind and its faculties being lax and heedless, allowing thoughts to wander toward external conditions, contemplating literature and arts, worldly skills and crafts, and various unwholesome reflections and investigations (*vitarka-vicāra*).

Master An of Guangxiao Monastery in the Song dynasty saw two monks leaning against a railing and conversing while he was in meditative concentration (*samādhi*); initially, there were celestial beings (*deva*) surrounding them.
Wei listened attentively. After a long time, they dispersed. Shortly thereafter, malevolent spirits spat and cursed them, sweeping away their footprints.

When he inquired about the reason for this, it was revealed that the two monks had initially discussed the Buddha-dharma, but their discourse became disjointed and eventually turned to matters of livelihood.
From that time on, Dao’an never again spoke of worldly affairs for the rest of his life. As the Vinaya states: "There were two bhikṣus traveling along a road who spoke [of such things]."
This was improper speech. At that time, there was a yakṣa without faith who wished to suck away his vital essence.
The Buddha said: "When a bhikṣu travels on the road, he should contemplate wholesome dharmas. There are two kinds of practice: first, engaging in proper speech; second, noble silence.
Upon reaching a place of rest, one should recite the noble gāthās. Nowadays, people spend their entire day in idle chatter and miscellaneous talk—how much more so [should they avoid such things]!
One cannot avoid the reproaches of gods and ghosts; how much less can one hope for their protection?
Thus, in the pursuit of pleasure for a single lifetime, one fails to realize that such pleasure is the cause of suffering.

The first line clarifies indulgence and pleasure; the second line clarifies the cause of suffering. This means that if one in this life gives rein to the passions and indulges in sensual pleasures, these are precisely the causes of future suffering.
When the causes of suffering thus accumulate, the fruits of suffering will inevitably arrive.

Therefore it is said: "If the ground is not true, the fruit will be circuitous. That which is met with in the present as retribution, and that which leads to sinking and wandering after death—this is what is meant by this.
Regarding "a single lifetime": although the lifespans of sentient beings who receive a body differ in length, they are all the karmic retribution of a single period.
Thus, seeking pleasure throughout one life truly constitutes the calamity of suffering for ten thousand kalpas.
The commentary states: "Sensual pleasures" refers to the pleasures of the five desires.
Throughout past kalpas, one has pursued worldly dust without ever reflecting upon it.

The first phrase clarifies following the habits of sensory objects; the second phrase clarifies the loss of the eye of wisdom. Since beginningless kalpas, [the mind] has been directed exclusively toward...

Following the habitual tendencies of one's own delusions, they chase after the false objects of the various sensory realms; until now, these have burned fiercely within the breast, never for a single thought-moment having been reflected upon to recognize their error.
How, then, could one be able to diligently cultivate concentration and wisdom to shatter those delusive habits and emerge from the toils of worldly existence?
The commentary states: *Nang* (曩) refers to the past; *kalpa* (劫) signifies a long duration, meaning from time immemorial. *Chen* (塵) means dust or defilement, carrying the sense of pollution.

This refers to the various delusive objects and the habitual tendencies of affliction (*kleśa-vāsanā*), which are able to pollute the true nature of one's own mind, thereby preventing the realization of the Way.
"Time is submerged; years are wasted.
The former phrase refers to the loss of days and nights; the latter refers to the loss of months and years. "Submerged" means to be obliterated;
"wasted" means to let time pass in vain. If one does not single-mindedly cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom, one will not only bury one's precious time.
In truth, this is merely to waste a hundred years.

The *Ji* (Record) states: "The phrase 'time and light' refers to the alternating presentation of day and night. Here, "time" refers to the twelve *zhī* and *gān* (the twelve earthly and heavenly stems), while "light" refers to the three luminaries.
The enjoyments are abundant and the benefits of giving are rich.

The first phrase refers to one's own use; the second phrase refers to what is given by others. Others bestow gifts upon them without weariness in their pursuit of merit, yet the recipients must give rise to a sense of shame and modesty, knowing the proper measure in their enjoyment.
As for "enjoyment," it means that the body and mind receive nourishment and one partakes of these things according to one's inclination.
"Generosity" (*dāna*). "Abundant" (*yinfan*) means that the four types of offerings are plentiful and the one hundred and one requisites are fully provided.
"Benefit through generosity" (*shili*) refers to the fourfold offerings and the one hundred and one necessities. "Abundant" and "thick" (*nonghou*) differ in name but are identical in meaning.
The record states: Dharma Master Huixiu wore a single pair of shoes for thirty years; whenever he encountered soft ground, he would go barefoot.

He once instructed the assembly, saying: "You now enjoy all manner of comforts—eating before you are hungry, dressing before you are cold, bathing before you are soiled, and sleeping before you are weary.
Yet your eye of the Way is not yet clear and the outflows of your mind are not yet exhausted. How can you bear this?"
"Yin" means flourishing; "fan" means abundant. "Nong" means not bland; "hou" means not thin.
The "four offerings" are food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine. The "one hundred and one items" are the requisites for the sustenance of a śramaṇa’s body.
It has passed through years and decades, yet there was no intention to abandon it.

The first phrase refers to time; the second phrase refers to the mind. Because one’s enjoyment was so abundant and one indulged in its flavors without ceasing, one unconsciously experienced the passage of years and decades, never once giving rise to a single thought of renunciation or weary detachment.
The commentary states: "To 'simulate' (ni) means to simulate [the action] before performing it; that is, to deliberate and wait. Master Fuyong said:
'If one seeks to escape birth and death out of weariness with worldly toil, one must let the mind rest and cease discursive thoughts, severing all attachments to external conditions.'"
Therefore, it is called "leaving home. How could one allow trivial gain and honor to bury one's entire life?

One must simply cast both ends open and let go of the middle. Encountering sounds or forms, be like planting flowers upon a stone; encountering profit or fame, be like having a speck of dust in the eye.
Furthermore, from time immemorial, there is nothing you have not already experienced—why need you suffer so?
How bitter is this craving! If one does not cease now, when will one ever do so?
Accumulations grow ever more numerous as one maintains this illusory form.

The first phrase refers to amassing non-durable things; the second refers to nourishing a dream-like, phantom body—meaning that one accumulates the four types of offerings, which are themselves insubstantial.
These riches merely maintain the illusory substance of the five aggregates, which are like dreams. Once impermanence arrives, what use is all that has been accumulated?
