When the four elements disperse, where can that which was preserved remain? Thus, the *Nettippakaraṇa* states: "Life cannot be guaranteed, yet one strives only to provide for it;
death is certain to arrive, yet one knows not how to look toward it. How much more so this precarious life, subject to calamity and impermanent change!"
In the space of a mere moment, he died suddenly and unexpectedly. Yet, as his evil causes had already accumulated, his evil retribution was difficult to escape;
that the shape of the form determines the distortion of the shadow—is this not a statement free from falsehood?

The record states: "Wealth belongs to the five families; therefore, it is called 'not firm. This refers to being swept away by water, consumed by fire, stolen by bandits, seized by officials, or ruined by wicked sons.
Chan Master Wuzuo said: "If blessings are inferior while wealth is excessive, that wealth will surely become a calamity.

If virtue is meager while the burden is great, that burden will quickly bring about harm. The ancients desired only for the mind to be realized, not for the body to be realized. They were truly worthy.
Do not conceal [your faults]; do not boast of your virtues. If you act in this manner, you will know your destiny, accord with the Way, and preserve yourself throughout your entire life.
The Master has issued a decree to exhort the bhikṣus: advance in the Path and cultivate yourselves with solemnity; in these three matters, one is never sufficient.
The first two lines are an exhortation; the latter two lines demonstrate the Dharma. The Tathāgata is the Dharma-King of the three realms and the Teacher of the fourfold assembly.
Having exhausted the nature of all phenomena, he observes the capacities of beings to bestow the Dharma accordingly, administering medicine according to the ailment.

Therefore, he establishes the teachings and formulates the precepts, commanding his disciples to practice and advance on the Path, requiring that they be diligent, have few desires, and possess knowledge.
It is sufficient to adorn one's person with three things. These three things are: food and drink, clothing, and sleep.

These three cause people to be obscured; they are the causes and conditions that obstruct the Path. Therefore, one must always remain insatiable regarding them before one can be in harmony with the Path.
The commentary states: "The Guide" refers to one who leads sentient beings out of the burning house of the three realms. The *Suyāma-sūtra* says:
"Because he gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, causing them to enter the right path, and does not seek any recompense for his kindness, he is called the Guide.
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-hṛdaya-sūtra* says: "Because he shows the path to nirvāṇa, enabling them to attain the unconditioned, eternal bliss, he is so named."
The Great Teacher, in the *Teaching Left Behind by the Buddha*, said: "O bhikṣus, if you wish to be liberated from all suffering and affliction, you should contemplate contentment.
The dharma of contentment is itself the place of wealth, joy, peace, and security. For one who is content..."
Though one may lie upon the ground, it is still peaceful and joyful; yet for those who lack contentment, even dwelling in heaven does not satisfy their desires.
Those who lack contentment are poor despite their wealth; those who possess contentment are rich despite their poverty.
Those who lack contentment are constantly dragged about by the five sensual desires and are objects of compassion for those who possess contentment. You all, [should reflect] in this way...
"Kāśyapa, when you receive various foods and drinks, you should regard them as taking medicine. Whether they are good or bad, do not give rise to feelings of attachment or aversion.

Accept them merely to sustain the body and eliminate hunger and thirst. Just as a bee gathers nectar from a flower, taking only its flavor without damaging its color or fragrance, so too should a bhikṣu accept the offerings of others;
he should merely remove his own afflictions and must not seek much, lest he destroy his wholesome mind."
Furthermore, it says: "O bhikṣus, you should stroke your own heads, having abandoned ornaments and finery;

wear robes of dyed color and carry alms-bowls, sustaining yourselves by begging. It further says: "O bhikṣus, during the day, apply yourselves with diligence to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas and do not let the time pass in vain.
During the first and last watches of the night, do not allow for negligence. During the middle watch of the night, recite the sūtras."
Regulate yourself. Do not let the conditions of sleep cause this one life to pass in vain, resulting in nothing attained.
You should reflect that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds; seek early deliverance for yourself and do not sleep. "Exhort" (*mǔ*) means to encourage and spur oneself on;
"vigilance" (*yán*) means to be solemn and upright.
Many people here indulge in these flavors without ceasing; as days pass and months come, suddenly their heads turn white.

The first two lines describe the craving for profit; the latter two lines describe the forgetting of life. Alas! While attachment to worldly gain has not yet ceased, one is unaware that white hair has already piled upon the head.
Days pass and months come like a whirling firebrand; the tally of death is not far off and will soon arrive.
"Arrival. The commentary states: "In this regard, there are three matters. 'Sā' (颯) is like the wind blowing suddenly;
as the *Āgama* Sūtra says, there are four matters that one does not announce to others beforehand: first, the graying of the hair; second, old age; third, illness; and fourth, death."
These four matters cannot be avoided, nor can they be repelled.
Those who have recently begun their studies and have not yet heard the essential meaning should extensively consult those who possess prior knowledge.

The first phrase speaks of the lack of benefit for others; the second phrase instructs one to first secure one's own benefit. This refers to a life lived in vain and aging in emptiness, of which there is no word [of praise].

To receive those who come after, if one wishes to benefit others, one must first benefit oneself. To benefit oneself, one must inquire extensively to gain prior knowledge and penetrate the source of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' mind-nature.
To benefit others, one must thoroughly understand the True Doctrine and widely demonstrate the gates of skillful means regarding phenomena and principle.

In extensive inquiry, one does not discriminate between the noble and the humble, nor does one feel shame in humbling oneself to seek instruction. This is what is meant by "relying on the Dharma rather than..."

Regarding the person: to demonstrate this extensively, one makes no distinction between enemy and friend, nor between noble and base. This is what is meant by a compassionate mind and upright conduct, bestowing the Dharma with equanimity.
Should one harbor thoughts of "self" and "other," both self and other are lost. As the *Dharmapada* says: "First rectify yourself, and then you may rectify others.
To discipline the body and enter into wisdom is surely the highest way. If the body cannot benefit itself, how can it benefit others?"

To benefit others, one must have a disciplined mind and a rectified body; what wish could then remain unfulfilled? Though one may recite a thousand words, if one does not practice them, what benefit is there?

It is better to hear but one word and diligently cultivate it to gain benefit. Though one may recite a thousand words, if one does not seek transcendence from the world, it is not as good as a single moment of awakening.

To utterly sever ties with the triple world: though one may recite a thousand words, if one does not maintain compassion and wisdom, it is not as good as listening once [to this teaching], which brings benefit to both oneself and others.

The Record states: "The 'Essential' (zhì) refers to the fundamental tenets of the Sūtras and Vinaya; the 'Tendency' (qù) refers to where those tenets ultimately lead. As for 'Tenet' (zōng), it means 'venerable'."
"Also. "Chong" (Veneration) refers to the essential meaning—the intent of what is venerated, honored, and emphasized within the Sūtras and Vinaya;

it is the ultimate point of convergence. "Broad" means extensive consultation; "questioning" means requesting further instruction. "Those who know first" refers to those who have attained prior awakening.
The *Shisao* states: "The ancients said that broad learning serves to alleviate poverty. The *Sengzhuan* states: "Without breadth, one's speech will lack [substance]."
This is the basis for my position. Therefore, one must never tire of extensive learning; through breadth, one attains mastery.

The Master said, "The gentleman extensively studies the cultural records and constrains himself with ritual propriety; in this way, he may not stray from the Way. Those who are born into poverty yet devoted to learning are but weaklings;
those who die wealthy in the Way are true gentlemen. Thus we know that extensive learning is what brings one's insight and vision to fulfillment.
This is their poverty. Zhuangzi said: "A person who does not study is called 'meat for the eyes' (a mere object of sight).
One who studies but does not practice is called 'a gathered bag' (one who merely collects knowledge). Not to rebel means not to deviate from the Way."

"Thinking that leaving the household life was for the sake of seeking food and clothing"—these two phrases serve as a transition from the preceding to the following section. "Thinking" (*jiang*) means desire, intention, or it is also a term of suppression.
However, in renouncing the secular world to leave home [as a monk], one fundamentally regards the Way as paramount; it is not that food and clothing are held in high esteem. The Record states:
Dharma Master Dao’an admonished the assembly, saying, "You have already left the household life, abandoning the secular world and bidding farewell to your sovereign.

You disregard wealth and beauty, and do not belong to the worldly crowd. You do not prize gold and jade, but hold only the Way as precious. Restrain yourself and maintain your integrity, finding sweetness in..."
Suffering, pleasure, and poverty. Drawing near to virtue, one delivers oneself and is further able to deliver others.
○ Sixth, the revelation of the Three Studies:
The Buddha first established the Vinaya to initiate and enlighten the ignorant.
The first line clarifies the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) and seven groups (*saptasaṃghāvaśeṣa*). The second line clarifies the awakening of those with beginner capacity (*ādikarmika*).

This is because the Vinaya is the foremost study for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and the foundation of all myriad virtues. "Ignorant" (*mōng*) refers to those who have not yet realized the stage of sainthood (*āryabhūmi*);
they are termed ignorant, let alone other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) on the stages of limited practice (*bhūmi*). Thus, the Buddha first established the Vinaya.

This is because the afflictions of sentient beings burn fiercely; the three poisons arise in competition, and through inverted and chaotic thoughts, they lose the light of wisdom and create the karma of birth and death.
Therefore, the Tathāgata establishes teachings according to their capacities: first, he uses the *vinaya* (moral discipline) to prevent wrongdoing and stop evil;
next, he uses meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to quiet the mind and forget external conditions; and finally, he uses wisdom (*prajñā*) to destroy delusions and realize the Truth.
Therefore, Mount Nan said: "Matters arising from body and speech are governed by the prevention of the precepts; yet the violent eruption of the three poisons is fundamentally driven by the mind.
Thus, one first seizes it with the precepts, next binds it with meditative concentration, and finally slays it with wisdom. Is this not the logical sequence?"
The commentary states: "Buddha" refers to our original teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata. In the Sanskrit language, he is fully called *Buddha*.

This means "the Knower" and also "the Awakened One. It signifies that beneath the Bodhi tree, he clearly and perfectly awakened to the knowledge of all phenomena—including whether sentient beings of the three periods of time are sentient or non-sentient, and whether they are permanent or impermanent—and thus his three types of awakening were perfectly luminous; for this reason, he is so titled.
To become a Buddha involves three aspects: first, self-awakening, which is to realize that one’s nature is truly eternal and to understand that delusions are empty and false;

second, awakening others, which is to employ unconditional compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*) to deliver the realm of sentient beings; and third, the perfection of awakened conduct, which means exhausting the source and reaching the ultimate depth so that practice is fulfilled and fruition is perfected.
The Sanskrit term *vinaya* is translated here as "discipline" (*lü*). "Discipline" (*lü*) means "to define" or "to measure," referring to the defining and weighing of the gravity of offenses.
Regarding "opening," "prohibiting," "maintaining," and "violating": the Sanskrit term *prātimokṣa* translates here as "individual liberation" (*bie jietuo*), which is precisely the precepts.
This refers to the three types of action and seven branches [of misconduct], each preventing what is non-virtuous and bringing about individual liberation.

Furthermore, once the precepts have been received, one refrains from committing acts such as killing; because there is no longer an individual cause, there is no longer an individual result. Therefore, it is called "individual."
"Deliverance" (*vimukti*). "Commencing" (*chàng*) means the beginning; it refers to the initial stage of establishing the Dharma and founding the work.
The five sections and seven groups are detailed in the *Mahāvinaya*. These consist of the two hundred and fifty precepts for *bhikṣus* and three hundred and forty-eight precepts for *bhikṣuṇīs*.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "The method for receiving the precepts for *bhikṣuṇīs* is five hundred in brief, and eighty thousand in detail."
Regarding "rules of conduct and dignified demeanor," they are as pure as ice and snow.
The first phrase indicates the Dharma; the second phrase provides a metaphor. "Rules of conduct" refers to the patterns and regulations of the Vinaya.
If a person can receive and uphold these rules, they will proceed directly toward the unsurpassed path. "Dignified demeanor" means possessing majesty...

They are formidable; they possess dignified decorum that inspires reverence. Because bhikṣus uphold the prohibitive precepts, their manifold virtues are majestic and awe-inspiring, causing others to regard them with fear.
In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, their deportment is upright and correct, causing others to revere them.
Thus, internally disciplined and externally correct, untainted by even a speck of dust, they are as pure as water and as white as snow.
The commentary states: The first two lines of the original text constitute the essence of the precepts (śīla-svabhāva); the following four lines constitute the function of the precepts.
They restrain the initial mind through the practice of cessation and observance (saṃvara-śīla) and the avoidance of transgression (asaṃvara-śīla).
The first line clarifies observance and transgression; the second line clarifies their functional efficacy. Now, cessation is itself observance, while action is transgression.

Through cessation, the three karmas do not race toward delusive objects and all evils fail to arise. Through observance, one maintains a firm and steadfast resolve, and the mind is freed from distraction and dissipation;
this constitutes self-restraint. It is the primary precept for entering the Way and the initial gateway to concentration and wisdom. Therefore—

This refers to the "beginner's mind. The Record states: "To 'cease' means that all evils do not arise; to 'maintain' means that no *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses) are committed. Furthermore, to 'cease' means the mind does not move falsely;
to 'maintain' means to hold fast without losing it. To 'bind' means that mindfulness is not dissipated; to 'collect' means the water of concentration becomes limpid."
However, the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "There are those who say, 'What need is there to cling to the precepts in the Mahāyāna?
This is an error. To say one does not cling means that one upholds [the precepts] without clinging. If one were to call non-upholding 'not clinging,' that would be the destruction of clinging;
how then could it be called 'not clinging'? If even the act of holding them is absent, where can false adherence exist?"
The "Subtle Precepts" reform all vulgar abuses.

The first phrase clarifies the characteristics of the precepts; the second phrase clarifies their remedial application. Because these precepts encompass three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices, they are called the "Subtle Precepts.
Because they serve as the remedy for the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called...
To reform all that is vulgar and debased.
The Record states: "Articles" refers to the various subtle rules and characteristics within the two hundred and fifty precepts. "Reform" means to repent and eliminate.
"Vulgar and debased" refers to the habitual defilements of the various delusions, namely the three poisons and the ten fetters. These various delusions...
Briefly stated, there are the three fetters and the ten proclivities; extensively stated, there are the eighty-eight proclivities, up to the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).
These are able to bind sentient beings, driving them to wander through the three realms and preventing their liberation.

The three fetters are: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); second, attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and third, the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*). To these are added greed, anger, delusion, pride, the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).

View (*dṛṣṭi*) and adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) constitute ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). These ten underlying tendencies, as they pass through the four truths of the three realms, differ in their increase and decrease, totaling eighty-eight underlying tendencies.

Specifically, under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all ten underlying tendencies are fully present. Under the two truths of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*), there are seven underlying tendencies each;

that is, the three underlying tendencies—view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—are excluded. [Under] the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*)...

Below [the desire realm] there are eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). That is to say, excluding the two proclivities of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), there are thirty-two proclivities when combined across the four truths.
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is exactly as in the desire realm regarding the four truths;

however, from each truth downward, one further excludes the proclivity of aversion (*pratigha*), because the proclivity of aversion does not function in these two upper realms. Thus, each realm has twenty [proclivities].
There are eight *anuśayas*. When combined with those of the two upper realms, there are fifty-six *anuśayas*;
together with the thirty-two *anuśayas* of the desire realm previously mentioned, they total eighty-eight *anuśayas*. Regarding the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśas*):

based on the modes of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the mode of equal proportions, each possesses twenty-one thousand varieties, totaling eighty-four thousand. [The three thousand majestic...]

Regarding the eighty thousand subtle practices: there are two hundred and fifty rules of training (*śikṣāpada*). Since there are two hundred and fifty for each of the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—they total one thousand.
Following these through the three periods of past, present, and future, they become three thousand modes of deportment.
By applying these three thousand to the seven branches of body and speech, they constitute twenty-one thousand. By means of these...

These twenty-one thousand [teachings] further counteract the four types of afflictions—greed, hatred, delusion, and those in equal proportion—thereby constituting eighty-four thousand subtle practices.
These serve as the remedies for the eighty-four thousand gateways of worldly defilements.
Regarding the Dharma seat of the *Vinaya*, I have never had the honor of attending; as for the definitive meaning of the Supreme Vehicle (*yāna*), how could I possibly discern it?

This is a phrase indicating a causal relationship where the former gives rise to the latter: the first two lines concern not having practiced the precepts, while the latter two lines concern the inability to clarify the scriptural teachings.
"Never having had the honor of attending" means that one has never yet completed five summer retreats under a teacher or participated in ten formal assemblies.

Listen. Since the precepts are the foremost study of the Tripiṭaka and the initial gateway to meditative concentration and wisdom, how can one clarify the teachings and principles while attempting to leap over these stages?

If one has not even entered the first gateway, how can one ever peer into the inner sanctum? Thus we know that if the discipline of the precepts is not strict, true understanding and liberation will not arise.
Without the ultimate teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), how could one analyze and realize it? By "definitive meaning" is meant the teachings of the various Mahāyāna sūtras;
these are discourses that provide decisive resolution and clear exposition, extensively elucidating the meaning of the Middle Way and the true reality (*dharmatā*).
They are not like the sūtras of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) or other teachings that conceal the truth through indirect expressions and hidden intentions (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*).
The Record states: Master Zhongguo said, "As for the Dharma of the Chan school, one should rely upon the words of the Buddha.

Taking the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle as the basis, one realizes the original ground of the mind and transmits it from one to another, making it identical to the Way of the Buddhas. One must not rely on deluded sentiments."
Furthermore, to produce arbitrary interpretations of the teachings of provisional meaning and thereby mislead future students is of no benefit whatsoever.
It is like the parasites within a lion’s body that consume the lion’s own flesh; it is not the work of celestial Māras or external paths that can destroy the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the "Vinaya assembly," this refers to a place where the precepts are expounded. According to the Vinaya regulations, even if a bhikṣu has attained [realization]...

Even those possessing the three knowledges (*traividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) must remain under a teacher for five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*) to study the Vinaya. If one’s understanding of the Vinaya is not clear, one must not depart from the state of dependence (*niśraya*) even until the end of one’s life.
The *Zizhi* states: "The Vinaya prescribes that for five summer retreats or less, a bhikṣu must devote himself exclusively to the Vinaya section.

Only after he has mastered the observance and violation [of precepts] and is capable of performing the affairs of a bhikṣu may he then proceed to study the Sūtras and Śāstras. Now, this [practice] has been transgressed.
Next, one must study. If one’s practice loses its proper order, there will be no way to enter the Path. That the Great Sage’s reprimands were not in vain is evident.

Nowadays, as soon as one has barely received the precepts, one immediately proceeds to listen to the teachings and engage in Chan meditation. Yet, regarding the conduct and decorum of a monk, one understands nothing at all;
let alone showing contempt for the disciplinary rules and disparaging the *vinaya*, one deprecates the study of the Vinaya as being of the "Hīnayāna," while neglecting to uphold [the precepts].
The precepts serve as the standard for upholding [the Dharma]. Yet you remain mired in the confusion of worldly dust, indulging in your own stubbornness and obstinacy.
If the precepts may indeed be treated lightly, why did you ascend the altar to receive them? If the Vinaya may indeed be violated, why did you shave your head and don the dyed robes?

To treat the precepts lightly is entirely to slight yourself; to violate the Vinaya is likewise to destroy yourself. Delusive emotions are easy to habituate, but the Ultimate Way is difficult to hear.
To transcend the mundane and rise above the masses is a feat that occurs but once in ten thousand. I pray you examine the sacred instructions; can you not follow them?
As for those who attend ten sessions of lectures: in the past, Master Xuan was exhorted by his teacher to go and listen to the *Vinaya* ten times.

Master Xuan was certainly not dull-witted, yet he still attended ten times. This was because he wished to exhaust its subtle refinements and fully grasp its essential principles for the sake of meditative concentration and wisdom.
This is the foundation of the Way and the essential point of non-arising. To "discern" means to analyze and clearly understand the underlying principles.
It is a pity that one's entire life may pass in vain; once regret sets in, it is difficult to pursue.
These two phrases are words of lamentation. They mean that if the Sūtras and Vinaya are not clear, one loses the precepts of body, mind, and wisdom;
thus, the profound Way cannot be realized through any cause, and this constitutes a life lived in vain. When the cycle of birth and death reaches its end, it will be too late for regret;
therefore, it is said that [the opportunity] is difficult to pursue.

The Vinaya constitutes the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*). The Sūtras belong to the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*). Having thus concluded the exposition of these two trainings, what follows clarifies the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*);
for it is only through the sublime wisdom of the Path (*mārga*) that one can truly accord with and realize [the truth].
One has never applied oneself to the teachings and principles; there is no cause for awakening to the profound Way.

As for the first phrase, "wisdom and understanding are not yet complete," and the second phrase, "sudden awakening is impossible"—the term "teachings and principles" refers to that which explains the principle as the teaching, and that which is explained by the teaching as the principle.
The teaching that explains the principle consists of the twelve divisions of the scriptures. This is truly because...
The Tathāgata establishes his words based on principle, enabling sentient beings to practice and realize that principle. The *Sijiaoyi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings) states:

"It is called 'teaching' (*jiao*) because it expresses the principle that can be articulated, thereby transforming the minds of beings. There are three meanings to this transformation: first, transforming evil into good;
second, transforming delusion into understanding; and third, transforming the ordinary person into a sage. As for what is meant by "articulating the principle," it refers to...

It elucidates the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as well as the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*). As for the "Mysterious Path" (*xuándào*), it is the Mind-Seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
speaking figuratively, it is the path that is profound, subtle, wondrous, quiescent, and signless.

If one does not take the teachings and principles of the Tathāgata as the direct cause, then there would be no means for the sudden awakening to the unsurpassed, wondrous path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Therefore, Bodhidharma...
The Patriarch from the West took the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra* as his seal of the mind; the Fifth Patriarch of Huangmei exhorted the upholding of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*;
Tiantai entered realization through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; and Guifeng attained sudden awakening through the *Mahāśūnyatā-saṃdhinirmocana*. Thus, the *Zongjing lu* states:
"The various patriarchs of India, the six generations of this land, and even Mazu, Nanyang, Ehu, and Chan Master Kongsan [all followed these teachings]."
He was extensively versed in both the sutras and the śāstras and attained perfect realization of his own mind. All his instructions to disciples were supported by authentic evidence;
he never spoke from his own imagination or ventured arbitrary pronouncements. Consequently, as the years passed, the true spirit of the Dharma did not decline.
Taking the words of the Sages as the definitive standard, heterodoxy and falsehood could not shift him; using the orthodox teachings as his guide, he relied upon them with firm justification.

However, do not cling to the literal expressions of the teachings and allow views to arise merely following the words; you must directly investigate the underlying intent beneath the exegesis and harmonize with the fundamental school.
Then, teacherless wisdom will manifest before you and the natural, celestial Way will not be obscured. Thus, one knows that the teachings possess the power to assist the Path;
how could those of initial resolve ever forget them for a moment? For this reason, the successive patriarchs and former sages of antiquity—

There was none who did not investigate the ultimate principles of the Tripiṭaka until they were thoroughly mastered, thereby attaining confirmation within their own minds and transforming sentient beings according to the prevailing conditions. Those who study today cannot fully achieve this;
instead, they give rise to contempt and slander. What kind of mind is this? If one forgets the wicker trap after having caught the fish, what fault is there in the Sūtras and Vinaya?
Not a single word or syllable spoken by the Tathāgata’s golden mouth has been lost across hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes.

They have not even heard or seen [the teachings], much less been able to receive, uphold, understand, or realize them. Thus we know that the teaching does not delude people; rather, it is people who delude themselves regarding the teaching. Guifeng said:

"Under the gates of all the various schools, there are those who have attained realization. Yet each remains settled in what they have practiced; those who are comprehensive are few, while those who are narrow are many.

They take their own lineage of transmission as the door and window through which they look out, each opening wide for themselves. They take the sutras and śāstras as their weapons, clashing with one another."
They attack one another; their sentiments shift and change according to the bow and arrow [of debate]. Their methods rise and fall based on the notions of self and other.
This causes right and wrong to become entangled, such that no one can distinguish between them. The Sūtras are like a carpenter’s line and square, establishing what is heterodox and what is correct.
The line and square are not themselves clever; the clever artisan must rely upon the line and square. The Sūtras and Śāstras are not Chan; those who practice Chan must rely upon the Sūtras.
The Treatises serve as the standard. One should know that the Sūtras are the Buddha’s words, Dhyāna is the Buddha’s mind, and the Vinaya is the Buddha’s conduct.

The bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Tathāgata are fundamentally not in conflict with one another. It is simply because people and the Dharma have diverged, and the Dharma and people have fallen ill, that they abandon one and cling to another, thereby creating their own perversions.
If one were a person of ultimate realization who had turned all dharmas back upon themselves, then how could this be?
How could this not be so? What contradiction could there be? The Record states:
"The two phrases of the original text speak of the absence of the study of wisdom; this implies that there is no cause for sudden enlightenment.

Thus, one clarifies the teaching through the Vinaya, and one clarifies the Way through the teaching. Question: Sudden enlightenment is the essence of the school of direct pointing; it does not establish written words.
"What is the use of using the scriptures as a guide? He replied: "Have you not heard it said: 'To interpret the meaning based on the scriptures is the enemy of the Buddhas of the three ages;
to depart from even a single word of the scriptures is identical to the teaching of Māra'? Furthermore, it is said: 'People today who study the ancient teachings cannot avoid mental agitation;
yet if one wishes to avoid mental agitation, one must indeed study the ancient teachings. The *Pao-tsang lun* says: 'The ancients..."
A mirror reflects the essence; that essence manifests itself in form. Ancient teachings reflect the mind; that mind is itself luminous.

If one knows that all phenomena are fundamentally the wondrous functioning of the inherent virtues within the Tathāgatagarbha, then what is right and what is wrong? What need is there for words and letters?
As for the twelve divisions of the scriptures, these are the twelvefold classification of the teachings throughout the Tathāgata’s lifetime. They are unified [under this principle].
The Compendium of the Tripiṭaka: 1. Sūtra; 2. Geya; 3. Vyākaraṇa; 4. Gāthā; 5. Udāna;
6. Nidāna; 7. Avadāna; 8. Itivṛttaka; 9. Jātaka; 10. Vaipulya; 11.
Adbhutadharma; 12. Upadeśa. Master Zhong of Nanyang; Chan Master Dayi of Ehu; Sikong.
Master Shōsan Jōzen:
Seven. The fault of failing to practice and study;
even as one reaches an advanced age and long standing in the order, one remains empty-stomached and haughty at heart, refusing to draw near to virtuous friends and knowing only how to be arrogant.

The first two lines clarify the mark of the self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); the latter two lines clarify the mark of conceit (*māna*). Furthermore, the first line refers to one who is advanced in years and seniority yet lacks virtue;
the second line refers to one whose mind is haughty yet lacks the Way, hence being called "empty-bellied.
To refuse to associate with others is self-reliance; to know only how to be arrogant is to oppress others. Both of these belong to the mark of conceit. Now, there are six kinds of conceit.
1. Pride (*māna*): This refers to regarding oneself as superior among those who are one's equals. 2. Excessive pride (*atimāna*):
Originally, others are inherently superior to oneself, yet one forcibly claims to be superior to them. 3. Self-pride (*asmimāna*): This refers to relying on oneself to treat others with contempt.

4. Arrogant pride (*abhimāna*): Originally, one has not attained the Path, yet one claims to have attained it. 5. Inferior pride (*ūnamāna*): This refers to originally being without [virtue or attainment].
Yes. To boast out of self-conceit constitutes the six types of false pride (*mithyā-māna*), which refers to clinging to wrong views and looking down upon others.
Among these six types of pride, this belongs to *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride), *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"), and *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride).

The commentary states: "To be merely advanced in age while one's virtue does not match it, and to know only how to be haughty without possessing any Way worthy of veneration—'age' refers to the year of birth, and 'lunar age' (*la*) refers to the years since receiving the precepts. 'Intimacy' means being close to others; 'good companions' refers to virtuous friends.
'Haughtiness' means a lack of humility, which is to say, to treat others with contempt."
Unfamiliar with the teachings and discipline, they lack any sense of restraint.

The first phrase refers to the failure regarding the teachings and discipline; the second phrase refers to the failure regarding body and mind. Being unwilling to draw near to enlightened teachers and virtuous friends, how could they recognize the practice of the teachings and discipline?
Not understanding how to practice, how can they possibly collect and restrain their body and mind?

The commentary states: "The Teachings (Sūtras) prevent the three poisons; the Vinaya prohibits the seven branches [of misconduct]. 'Unfamiliar' means not yet recognizing [the rules]. 'Restraining and collecting' means gathering and withdrawing [the senses].
This refers to those who speak loudly or in a high voice, uttering words without moderation, and showing no respect for the senior, middle, or junior seats during Brahmin assemblies."
There is no difference. [The faults are: making noise with the bowl and alms-basin;

rising before others have finished eating. The first two phrases constitute a failure of verbal action (*vāg-karma*); the next two phrases constitute a failure of mental action (*manas-karma*), as well as a failure of ritual procedure (*vidhi*).

The final two phrases constitute a failure of physical action (*kāya-karma*), as well as a failure of decorum (*vinaya*). Because one does not know the laws and regulations, the three types of action lack discipline; therefore, this has resulted.

If one can restrain and collect [the mind], then there is no task that cannot be accomplished. As for the *brāhmaṇa*, they are the secular class of the Western lands (*paścimadeśa*), one of the four castes (*caturvarṇa*).
They honor only seniority by age and do not prize longevity of virtue; thus, there is no respect for the distinctions of "senior," "middle," or "junior" seats.
Some arrive first and claim the seat of honor, while others who arrive later sit at the back. Their assemblies lack regulation, and their clamor is manifold due to this.
There is no withdrawal or concealment;
therefore, it is no different from that. The record states: In Sanskrit, *brāhmaṇa* means "Pure Conduct" (*jingxing*) here, and is also called "Brahmacārin" (*fanzhi*).
As for the four castes: first, the Kṣatriya, the royal lineage; second, the Brāhmaṇa, the noble lineage; third, the Vaiśya, the merchants; fourth...
Śūdras are farmers. "Without measure" means they lack the standards of the Dharma. "Assembling" refers to gathering together, whether for sacrificial rites, seasonal festivals, or scholarly debates;

these are all without distinction, meaning there is no difference between them. Among those who have left the household life, seniority is determined by the number of years since ordination (precept-ordination age);
thus, their virtue is considered long-standing, and respect is accorded based on this rather than one's birth year.
Their coming and going are discordant; the essence of the monastic body is entirely absent.
The upper phrase fails in the Dharma, and the lower phrase fails in ritual decorum. In their comings and goings, not even a trace of rule remains—like a jade tablet that has lost its squareness;
hence, it is called "discordance. In movement and stillness, they do not possess even the slightest vestiges of dignified demeanor, like a gathering of Brahmins.
It is so. Therefore, it is said that they are "entirely out of harmony" (*quánwú*).
The *Jì* says: "To be 'in discord' (*guāi*) means to turn one's back on, or to deviate from [the Way]. To be 'angular' (*jiǎo*) means to be square. 'Square' (*fāng*) refers to the Dharma and the Way.

When one’s approach and departure are in discord, one’s actions and arrangements are consequently square [and off-course]. The body of a *guī* is round above and square below, symbolizing the compass and square of Heaven and Earth.

It is a matter of squareness and roundness. If a *gui* (sacrificial jade tablet) loses its squareness, it is no longer a *gui*; if a monk deviates from the Dharma, he is no longer a monk. Therefore, it is said that [the true essence] is entirely absent.
Rising and sitting with agitation disturbs the thoughts of others.

The first phrase refers to losing oneself; the second phrase refers to losing others. Because the three karmas are not restrained, one’s sitting and rising lack constancy, and one’s restlessness is manifold.
Thus, one causes others to stir their thoughts.
The commentary states: *Zhōng* (pronounced *zhōng*) means that when one is *zhōng*, the mind and intentions are restless and agitated;

the emotions are not at peace, and one’s deportment is uncharacteristic. Chan Master Cishou said: "If it causes a person to stir their thoughts, demonic obstacles easily arise. A multitude of voices can melt gold."
What joy is there in one's own home? Though one may perform much merit, it is not as good as avoiding transgressions. When thoughts stir in the darkness, one is personally oblivious and unaware;
yet as days pass and months come, the face turns yellow and the body grows thin.
If one does not maintain even the slightest rules or minor points of decorum, with what means can one restrain future generations? Novices will have no basis upon which to model themselves.

The first two phrases indicate that one has lost the standard for oneself; the latter two phrases show that one cannot serve as a model for others. Since one does not personally maintain these rules...
The Dharma. How can one who does not practice the Dharma themselves serve as a model for others? Therefore, those who come to study have no basis from which to take a standard.

The *Ji* (Commentary) states: "New learners" refers to beginners; "later generations" refers to later worthies, meaning later students. To "imitate" is synonymous with taking [the Dharma] as a model. The *Book of Documents* says:

"If one does not guard against minor transgressions, they will eventually bring ruin to great virtue. This is true even for the Confucian scholars of the world; how much more so for those who have left it?
As for this "household," as soon as they perceive one another, they immediately say, "I am a mountain monk.
In the first phrase, they seek to establish the other; in the second phrase, they disparage themselves. They claim the other is virtuous and wish to support them with kind words, yet—
Out of his own inclination, he gave rise to conceit and thus uttered these shameless words.
The record states: "When he says 'I am a mountain monk,' he means he is one who dwells in the mountains;
he knows only a single *huatou* (critical phrase), and does not care for the sutras, the vinaya, or matters of dignified deportment and minute conduct. Master Fachang said: "There is one..."
"O Han! Take note of this bellyful of entanglements. Licking your lips and rubbing your mouth, you babble in barbarian tongues and Chinese alike, claiming, 'I understand Zen, I understand the Way.
You treat good people with contempt and commit the karma of the Avīci Hell.

One day, when the light from your eyes falls to the ground and the realm of karma manifests before you, you will be like a crab falling into boiling water—your hands flailing and your feet scrambling; all the clever schemes you have previously learned will be of no use at all."
Do not be attached. If you hear someone mention the private affairs of another, and anger and resentment arise, you might say, "How could there be such things in the Buddha-dharma?
Great enlightenment does not concern itself with minor details. Such people are like those who compare cow dung to sandalwood;
what connection can there possibly be between them? Master Cijue said: "Or perhaps one relies on one's own natural spontaneity and denies the existence of causes."
As for the fruit [of such practice], they falsely claim it flows only from within the chest, without relying on the stages and positions of cultivation.

Thus, the "Dharma Masters of coarse understanding" lack the eye of scriptural penetration, and the "vain Chan practitioners" do not value the gate of practice. This is the sin of partiality and deficiency.
Alternatively, their entire bodies may be shattered and their faces covered in dust; they possess none of the three thousand subtle conducts, nor the eighty thousand...
Their dignified deportment is entirely lacking. Some attend to social affairs or manage their disciples;

their bodies wander through the marketplace while their minds are stained by the ways of the common folk. Thus, the ordinary monks of the mountains and fields cannot escape the reproach of being like farmers.
That a Buddhist disciple would become an object of shame for a Confucian scholar is the fault of indolence.
Below, the text points out the causes of such lack of refined conduct and laziness.
Having never heard the Buddhist teachings on practice, one’s disposition has consistently remained coarse and impulsive.

The first phrase indicates a failure in hearing and cultivation; the second phrase indicates a failure in precepts and meditative concentration. Since the laws and regulations have not been heard, how can one know how to practice?
Since precepts and concentration have not been cultivated, one’s temperament remains like that of a monkey or a horse.
The commentary states: “Hearing” refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); “practicing and upholding” refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Although there are three types of wisdom—hearing, reflection, and cultivation—here the mention of hearing and cultivation subsumes reflection. All three are termed “wisdom” because each of these three factors can individually give rise to untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-ārya-prajñā*).
If one lacks this wisdom, one will be unable to sever afflictions and realize the truth.
Such a view and understanding arises because the beginner is indolent and given to gluttony and complacency.

The first phrase serves as a transition from what precedes to what follows; the second phrase refers to a lack of diligence in entering the Way; and the third phrase refers to wasting one’s days through greed for gain.
"Such a view and understanding" refers to the perceptions and insights of the aforementioned evil habits. This is indeed due to the indolence of the beginner.
Regarding "laziness and so forth": this refers to being indolent because one does not apply diligent effort when first entering the Path; hence, it is called "sloth and laziness.

Having failed to hear and practice the Buddha's teachings, one instead greedily pursues fame and profit and refuses to associate with virtuous friends. Consequently, one passes the days in negligence;
defiled conditions gradually deepen, and evil habits flourish, leading to such perceptions as these. This is precisely what is meant by "striking [the mind]."
The head does not encounter a master. The record states:
*yōng* (pronounced *róng*) means indolence; *tāo* (pronounced *tāo*) means greed for wealth; *tiè* (pronounced *tiě*) means greed for food.
The *Dharmakṣaya-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "When the Dharma is about to perish, various demonic śramaṇas will corrupt and disrupt my Way.
They will don secular clothing and take pleasure in the five-colored robes of the kāṣāya. They will not cultivate the precepts;
though they recite the precepts every half-month, they will be weary and indolent, having no desire to hear them. They will take no delight in reading or reciting the sūtras and vinaya."
Should there be readers who do not understand the words and phrases, yet insistently claim this to be so;

who do not consult those of clear insight, but out of arrogance seek fame, feigning an air of refined elegance as a mark of honor and nobility, hoping for offerings from others—upon the end of their lives and after death, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
Among the five heinous crimes, they will pass through the realms of hungry ghosts and animals without exception, for an infinite duration.
After undergoing punishment for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he was born in a borderland where the Three Jewels do not exist, just as the Buddha had predicted.
Even now, when the precepts are recited half-monthly, it is rare to find such a place; how much more so to actually hear them being recited?
Alas! This is truly a sign of the extinction of the Dharma. Formerly, Sengyun of the Qi dynasty resided at Baoming Monastery in Ye, becoming renowned for his lectures and expositions.

He mastered the essential principles of all doctrines. On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, during the assembly for the recitation of the precepts, Sengyun sat at the head of the assembly and addressed the monks, saying:
"The purpose of the precept texts is to prevent wrongdoing; since everyone can recite them, why trouble ourselves with hearing them repeatedly?"
He ordered a monk to expound the principles of the Dharma so that future generations might attain awakening; none among the assembly dared to oppose him.
Consequently, the recitation of the precepts was suspended until the morning of the fifteenth day of the seventh month. Suddenly, Yun’s whereabouts were lost.
The assembly searched for him in all directions and found him inside an ancient tomb about three li outside the monastery. His body was covered in blood. When asked the reason for this, he said:
There was a valiant warrior who, grasping a great sword in his hand, rebuked him with a fierce voice, saying:
"Who are you that dares to disrupt the *poṣadha* and falsely establish your own doctrines? I shall immediately strike down your body with this blade! The pain and agony were unbearable;

he was supported back to the monastery, where for ten years he practiced sincere repentance, recited the precepts and performed the *poṣadha* with utmost devotion, and studied and recited the various sūtras.
He took this as his constant practice. On the day of his death, a rare fragrance came to welcome him, and he passed away with joy.

At that time, everyone praised him for reforming himself while still in the world and for not failing in the constant patterns of human relations. Furthermore, there was the monk Fan of Dajue Temple, whose virtue in observing the precepts was pure and lofty.

Once, while staying overnight at another temple on the fifteenth day of the month, the assembly deliberated and collectively decided to suspend the *poṣadha* ceremony so that a monk might deliver a formal discourse (*dharmakathā*).
A monk ascended the seat and stated: "Establishing a discussion on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) deeply accords with the intention of the Sage;
why labor over the *poṣadha*, which is something monks hear constantly? Suddenly, he saw a deity over ten feet tall, majestic and awe-inspiring, who asked the one delivering the discourse:
"What day is it today? he asked. The answer was, "It is the *poṣadha* day. The spirit then struck him with his hand, dragged him beneath his seat, and beat him until he was nearly dead.
He then questioned the senior monk (*sthavira*), and the answer was the same as before; he struck him again and nearly killed him.

After having thus assaulted two or three senior monks, the spirit shook its arms and departed. At that time, both the monastics and the laity witnessed this together. When Master Fan saw this, because...
This was his lifelong self-exhortation. Whether in monastic affairs or private matters, he never dared to voice his own desires.

Even when his illness became so severe that he could no longer endure being carried on a litter, he requested that monks come to his room to reverently recite the precepts. At that time, he held the study of Sūtras and Śāstras in high esteem, while specializing in the school of Chan.
As for those who treat the precepts lightly, please observe this and reflect upon it:
as they drift through human life, they eventually become coarse and uncultivated; before they realize it, their feet have grown weary and old, and they face a wall whenever they encounter matters.
The first two lines involve the secular world and become wild; the latter two lines empty old age through a lack of discernment. Furthermore, the first line refers to mutual perfuming;
the second line refers to the formation of habits; the third line refers to the sudden arrival of decay; and the fourth line refers to the obscuration of the future by darkness.

This is because one does not cultivate right practice, but instead remains distracted and self-indulgent, daily entangled in worldly conditions, clinging to sensory objects, and giving free rein to the six passions.
Therefore, practicing with such a sincere heart ultimately results in becoming coarse and wild. As defilements deepen day by day, one lacks the power of contemplative insight;
how could one perceive the shifting flow of the four phases [of life]? Suddenly, the time of old age arrives; the path of the mind is blocked, and out of a hundred things, not one is understood.

When beholding objects, one encounters obstructions, like a person facing a wall. All of this arises from a refusal to seek broad knowledge from those who have already attained realization; thus, one reaches this state.
In the end, it becomes nothing but a relic. The record states:
"Rénrǎn" (荏苒) means to gradually spread and encroach. "Lùzhòng" (躙踵) refers to being unable to move forward. "Xiǔ" (朽) means decayed;
this refers to what is called an old vessel that no longer possesses the three flavors. It lives in vain and dies in vain, a useless waste of one's life.
Regarding the "three kinds of flavors" being absent: it is like sugarcane; once it has been pressed, the residue has no flavor remaining.

When the vigor of youth and the fullness of one's complexion have been crushed by old age, the three kinds of flavors are likewise absent. First, one is unable to recite the sūtras or explain their meaning.
Second, they are unable to practice seated meditation and contemplation; third, they are unable to perform meritorious deeds through labor.

As for the "four characteristics," they are arising, abiding, change, and cessation. Regarding the term "gudong" (antiques/curiosities), the *Motan* (Ink Talk) states that it was a name coined by the elder Luofu Ying for the act of cooking various foods together;
nowadays, it is frequently borrowed in common parlance.
When later students come for consultation, he does not respond with words to guide them. Even if he does speak, his discourse does not touch upon the canonical scriptures.
With the first two lines, he fails to provide nourishment and benefit; with the latter two lines, his speech has no relation to the classics.

Being thus like one facing a wall when encountering matters, how can he guide future generations? Even if he utters a single word or half-phrase, it bears no relation to the models and patterns established by the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
How is this different from the old crane that did not see the water?
The Record states: Not long after the Tathāgata had passed away, there was a bhikṣu who mistakenly recited a verse from the *Dharmapada* as follows:
"If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not see an old crane by the water, it would be better to live for but a single day and attain such understanding.
When the Venerable Ānanda heard this, he sighed sorrowfully and said, "How swiftly the True Dharma of the Tathāgata will perish!
He then spoke to that bhikṣu, saying: "As the Buddha has taught: 'If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not see...'"
"The Dharma of arising and ceasing is not like [the passing of] a single day, yet one may attain its clear realization. This bhikṣu offered this dedication to his teacher, who said:
"Ānanda is old and decrepit; his words are full of errors and should not be trusted. You should return to reciting as before.
According to the records of the past when the True Dharma still endured, such corruptions already existed; how much more so now, when the time since the Sage departed is so remote?
Without associating with virtuous friends or drawing near to enlightened teachers, how could one produce speech that accords with the classical canons?
Yet, when their words are slighted, they immediately reproach the juniors for being impolite; anger and resentment arise, and their speech becomes offensive toward others.

The first phrase refers to being censured for lacking virtue; the second phrase refers to failing to reflect upon one’s own faults; and the final two phrases refer to the poison of anger wounding others.
Since one’s words do not even touch upon the classics, what is there to wonder at in others’ disdain? Failing to reflect on one’s own faults, one instead rebukes the errors of others.
Once the fire of anger is unleashed, there is nothing it does not consume.
The commentary states: "Dveṣa" means anger; it is resentment and indignation. Furthermore, to be angry with others is *dveṣa*, while to be angry with oneself is *āghāta*.
Master Dao’an said: "When the Way is not understood through the sutras and preceptual virtue is entirely absent, one is ridiculed by friends and abandoned by fellow students."
Thus, having left the household life, one merely wastes their allotted years.

When the fruits of the eight karmas ripen, one suddenly lies ill upon a bed, entangled and oppressed by manifold sufferings; from dawn until dusk, one reflects with a heart full of agitation and terror.
The first two lines refer to physical suffering; the latter two lines refer to mental suffering. When the time for karmic retribution arrives, the four great elements lose their equilibrium.

If even one element is disordered, the hundred meridians and sinews contract. Lying prostrate upon the pillow in deep reflection, there is no good deed to recall; one is rendered helpless at the gate of the underworld.
What doubt could there be? Is this not a state of utter terror? The record states:
*ying* (縈) means to wind around and bind; *chan* (纏) means to entangle and fetter; *bi-po* (逼迫) refers to being driven and coerced with such urgency that one finds no peace;
*xiao-xi* (曉夕) means morning and evening; *si-chun* (思忖) means to contemplate and deliberate.
"To be 'dismayed' means to be confused and terrified by urgency. The path ahead is vast and boundless;
one knows not where it leads. It is only from this point that one begins to know how to repent of one's transgressions. What is the use of digging a well when one is already thirsty?"
The first two lines concern not knowing where one is going; the latter two lines concern the regret that is too late once it has arisen.

On the perilous paths of the six realms and within the vast wilderness of birth and death, one does not know where one comes from, so how could one know where one goes? If one does not prepare in advance during the days ahead, what can be done when one regrets it at the last moment?
The Buddha said: "It is because of delusion (*moha*) that there is birth and death. What is delusion? It is fundamentally from delusion [that this arises].
Coming from the intermediate state, one is now born as a human being, yet remains deluded; the mind is neither understood nor opened, and one does not know where one shall go upon death.
This is precisely what is meant by "not knowing where one is headed."
The commentary states: The first phrase of the original text says that the three miserable realms and the six paths of rebirth are vast and boundless.
The second phrase says that the mind-consciousness does not know its place of departure. The third phrase says that one only begins to repent of former transgressions at the moment of death.

The fourth phrase employs a metaphor to clarify this. The *Śata-avadāna-sūtra* (*Baiyu jing*) says: "Long ago, there was a poor man in a foreign land who was skilled at imitating the cry of a mandarin duck."

Desiring to steal a lotus flower, he entered the king’s pond and imitated the cry of a ruddy sheldrake (*cakravāka*). At that time, the keeper of the pond became suspicious and asked, "Who is in the pond?
The poor man, losing his composure, replied, "I am a ruddy sheldrake. The keeper then seized him.
He was about to go to the king’s presence when, midway there, he again began to cry out like a ruddy sheldrake. The guard said, "You did not do this before;
what benefit is there now? Foolish people of the world are just like this: they commit various evil deeds throughout their entire lives.
One does not habituate the mind’s activities to make them disciplined and virtuous. When the time of death arrives, one only then says, "I now wish to cultivate goodness.
But by then, the wardens of hell have already taken one away and delivered one to King Yama.
Although one wishes to cultivate goodness, it is of no avail—just like that foolish man who, upon reaching the king's presence, only then begins to coo like a mandarin duck.
I regret that I did not cultivate myself early on; in my later years, I have committed many transgressions. At the moment of death, I am distracted and wavering, filled with fear and terror.
The first two lines express self-reproach; the latter two describe losing one's master.

If the three poisons are not eliminated before the day arrives, and if one has accumulated sins like a mountain by late life, then when the final moment comes and the realms of karma appear before one, even if one tries to assert control by force, it will be difficult to avoid [the consequences].
"Trembling with fear and panic" refers precisely to the instability of one's heels on the day before [death], when one’s hands and feet become flustered at the moment of departure.
The commentary states: "Guo-zhou" (過咎) means transgression or fault. "Huo" (霍) should be read as "huo" (攉), which denotes the turning over of the hand.

To wave the hand is called "hui" (揮); to turn the hand back is called "huo" (攉). This refers to the swiftness of a palm-flip. As for "trembling with fear and panic": [it describes the state of agitation].
Extreme fear and agitation cause great haste.

When the silken net is torn and the sparrows fly away, the conscious mind follows its karma. It is like a person burdened with debt; the stronger creditor pulls them forward first. The mental continuum has many directions, yet it falls precipitously toward whichever part carries the greatest weight.

The first two lines describe how body and mind follow karma; the next two lines show how karma powerfully drags the mind along; and the final two lines indicate that the partiality of retribution arises specifically from the gravity of the mind.
Furthermore, the first line is a metaphor for the exhaustion of the fruits of prior karma; the second line shows the mind following karma as it departs;

the third and fourth lines are metaphors for strong karma preceding the retribution; the fifth line illustrates that deluded thoughts are not singular; and the sixth line shows that retribution falls from the mind. However...
The strength or weakness of wholesome and unwholesome karma depends upon the mind; as for the place of retribution, its lightness or gravity is determined by oneself.

If the defiled mind is turbid and heavy, one immediately falls into the three miserable realms; if wholesome karma is light and buoyant, one ascends to the human or celestial realms. According to the supramundane Dharma, however:
Human and celestial realms are originally the fruits of outflows (*āsrava*); they are also termed "falling. Only when the single mind does not arise can one escape from this descent.
Regarding the phrase "the silk is pierced and the bird flies away": the bird is a small bird. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "A bird enters a jar;
the mouth of the jar is covered with silk. When the silk is pierced, the bird flies away. Consciousness follows karma as it runs. Now, by means of...

The jar is a metaphor for the four great elements; the fine gauze is a metaphor for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); and the bird is a metaphor for the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna-ātman*). This consciousness-spirit is precisely the conscious mind.
Because it comes to receive retribution by riding upon its prior wholesome or unwholesome karma, it is like a bird entering a jar. Being bound by karma is like being veiled by the gauze.
When the retribution is exhausted, one immediately follows according to karma, like the bird departing when the gauze is pierced. Once departed, one must inevitably pursue one's karma.
Therefore, it is called "following after. Because the consciousness-mind is bound by the rope of karma within the vessel of form, there is nowhere it does not go.
As long as the rope of karma is not severed, having gone away, it returns again. When the vessel is broken and the bonds are severed, it departs and does not return;

this refers to when the present four great elements perish, which is called "having gone," and subsequently receiving a later body, which is called "returning" until [the state of] non-existence is reached.
Only when the fruit of learning is attained is the jar said to be broken. When the karma of future births is exhausted, it is called "non-return.

As for what is termed "consciousness-mind," this refers to the eighth mind-king, the *ālaya-vijñāna*. It maintains the seeds of good and evil and serves as the sovereign of the collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*).
"Karma according to [one's actions]" refers to the karma of good and evil created by the six consciousnesses, which is capable of leading the eighth consciousness through the six realms of existence.
One receives the body of collective retribution; karma acts as the projector, and consciousness is that which is projected. Therefore, it is said to "follow karma.

Regarding "that which first draws [one along]," this refers to the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome. Whichever is more powerful and weighty will first draw one forward, and one will then receive the retribution of the future.
Regarding "mental states" and so forth: this refers to the sixth consciousness. Its various delusive thoughts and discriminations are manifold;

it clings to the objects of the six sense-fields and performs numerous evil karmas, thereby falling into the three miserable realms. If such mental activity is excessive, one falls heavily; if delusive thoughts are few, one falls lightly.
Guifeng said: "To perform an act that is meaningful is the mind of awakening; to perform an act that is meaningless is the mind of distraction.

A distracted mind follows along with emotions, and at the moment of death, one is dragged away by karma. An awakened mind does not follow emotions, and at the moment of death, one can transform karma.
If you wish to verify whether or not you will have mastery over rebirth at the time of death, simply examine the dust-like thoughts of your ordinary mind."
Whether the objective realm is free or not free—this you must examine and reflect upon throughout the two periods of six hours each day.
This is Guifeng’s single dose of “sweat-inducing powder. O virtuous ones, examine yourselves well; do not let this opportunity slip away.

The commentary states: *Ālaya* is here translated as the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*). This means it is able to contain and store the seeds of all phenomena—both wholesome and unwholesome, mundane and supramundane.
Because, from the very beginning, the mind moved through non-awakening, thereby forming ignorance (*avidyā*) which perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness) and becomes the *ālayavijñāna*.
By grasping and maintaining these seeds, it is able to cause the cycle of birth and death to flow on.
It is uninterrupted; therefore, this consciousness is also called the "appropriating consciousness" (*ādāna-vijñāna*) or the "retribution consciousness" (*vipāka-vijñāna*).

This means it is the ripened fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma that draws forth birth and death. As for "ripening" (*vipāka*), it refers to performing an action in this life and receiving its retribution in a future life;
because the cause perishes and the fruit arises at a different time, it is said to "ripen. This corresponds to what was formerly called "fruit-retribution" (*vipāka-phala*). *Zongjing lu*, Question:

Question: At the time when the faculties decay and consciousness migrates away, one abandons this current body and receives another form. What are the characteristics of this consciousness as it comes and goes?
Answer: As stated in the *Vijñānakāya-sūtra*, the movement, migration, extinction, and coming and going of consciousness are like the element of wind (*vāyu-dhātu*).
It is colorless and formless, cannot be manifested, yet it is capable of setting all things in motion.
Objects manifest various forms; they may shake or stir the forests, breaking and shattering them while emitting great sounds.
Or they become cold or hot, touching the bodies of sentient beings to produce suffering or joy. Wind has no hands, feet, or physical appearance, nor does it possess colors such as black or white.
The realm of consciousness is likewise: it is without color, without form, and without luminous manifestation.
Due to the conditions of perfuming causes, various functional activities are manifested. The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states:

"After sentient beings have cast off this body, they are blown by the power of the winds of karma; consciousness is shifted and carried away, whereby they undergo the fruits of the karma they themselves have experienced.
[The term] *hu* (pronounced *hú*) refers to thin gauze, specifically square-mesh gauze.
The ghost of impermanence slays without ceasing from moment to moment; life cannot be prolonged, and time cannot be waited for.
The first two lines show that impermanence is swift; the latter two lines show that both time and life are swift. Thus, impermanence is treated as a murderous ghost.
This refers to impermanence (*anitya*). Although it has no form or substance that can be seen, it is able to sever the life-root (*jīvitendriya*) of human beings;

therefore, it is called the "Killing Ghost" (*māra*). The *Zhiguan* says: "The ghost of impermanence employs [beings] without distinguishing between the noble and the eminent. It is perilous, fragile, and not firm; it is difficult to rely upon.
How can one remain at ease, planning for a hundred years, racing about in the four directions to seek, store, and amass? To amass—[is to accumulate].

It is not yet enough. Suddenly departing for eternity, all one's wealth and possessions will merely become the property of others. One departs alone into the darkness; who will inquire into right and wrong?
That which "ceases to stop moment by moment" refers to the meaning of impermanent flux and non-abiding. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Impermanence is of two kinds: first, the impermanence of the destruction of the continuity of phenomena; second, the impermanence of moment-to-moment arising and ceasing.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "When a bodhisattva cultivates the perception of death, he contemplates this life-span as being constantly surrounded by immeasurable enemies.
It diminishes from moment to moment and never increases, like a mountain torrent that cannot remain still."
It is also like morning dew; its duration cannot last long. It is like a prisoner heading toward execution, drawing closer to death with every step.
"Life cannot be extended" refers to life-span (*āyus*), which is the fixed retribution resulting from the maturation (*vipāka*) of prior karma; therefore, it cannot be prolonged.
"Time cannot be waited for" means that time consists of fleeting moments. Since this is the fixed retribution of prior karma, it cannot be altered by human effort.
To be set aside for later. As it is said: "The King of Hell has decreed that one shall die at the third watch; he will certainly not allow a person to remain until the fifth watch.
It is difficult to escape fixed karma—is this not what that means?

The Record states: "The feet and heels growing old and worn out—this is the suffering of aging. Lying ill upon one's bed—this is the suffering of sickness. The murderous ghost of impermanence—this is the suffering of death.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says: "At the time of the end of life, the 'sword-winds' (kṣuravāyu) all stir."
It would be like having a thousand sharp blades piercing one’s body; even sixteen parts of that [suffering] do not equal one part [of the suffering in hell].
If there is any wholesome karma, then the affliction will be slight.
Among humans and devas within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), one should not yet be exempt from them. Such receiving of a body cannot be measured by kalpas;
the first two lines indicate that the fruits of karma are difficult to escape, while the latter two lines indicate that birth and death are without end.

By mentioning the "three existences," humans and devas are already included; however, to ensure that both the phrasing and the meaning are mutually clarified, they are stated redundantly. The "three existences" refers to the sentient beings of the three realms.
The causes of performed contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome and unwholesome karmas result in the attainment of future contaminated wholesome and unwholesome fruits and retributions.

Because cause and effect do not perish, it is called "existence" (*bhava*). First is *kāma-bhava* (desire-existence), which refers to the humans and devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as the sentient beings of the four miserable destinies;
because they are all not free from the defilement of desire, it is named desire-existence. Second is *rūpa-bhava* (form-existence), which refers to the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The heavens, although free from the defilement of desire, still possess material substance; therefore, they are called "existence with form" (rūpa-bhava). The three "formless existences" (arūpya-bhava) refer to the four heavens of the formless realm.
Since the four great elements have already ceased, there is no material substance; only the remaining four aggregates persist, and thus they are called "formless existence.
All of these are produced by causes as tainted results (āsrava-phala), bound by conditions, and are therefore conditioned (saṃskṛta); being so, they are impermanent.

Because one does not depart from taking birth within the three realms, it is said that one "should not yet be exempt" from this. When the fruit again creates a cause, and the cause in turn evokes a fruit, the cycle of saṃsāra is without end;
therefore, it is said that this cannot be measured by the number of kalpas.
The Record states: Regarding the number of kalpas, the world undergoes four phases—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness.
Each phase lasts for twenty minor kalpas (*antarakalpa*), so the four phases together comprise eighty minor kalpas.
One minor kalpa is calculated as 1,680,000 years; eighty minor kalpas constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). In total, this amounts to ten... [great kalpas].
Thirty-four million four hundred thousand years have passed; now, during the twenty minor kalpas of the human lifespan, a total of thirty-three million six hundred thousand years has elapsed.
This is currently the ninth minor kalpa, with eleven minor kalpas remaining.
Once these have passed, the time for the kalpa of destruction will arrive. The four aggregates refer to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Regarding these...

The six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu-deva*), the four evil destinies (*catur-apāya*), the four dhyāna heavens (*catur-dhyāna-bhūmi*), and the four formless heavens (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*) are all explained as below.

○ Ninth: Exhortation through diligent effort, cultivation, and the expression of sorrowful lamentation and astonishment. "How tragic!"—with such piercing urgency of heart, how could one remain silent? One must mutually admonish and encourage one another.
The first two lines express deep emotion; the latter two lines offer exhortation.

Because Guishan observed that in the Dharma-ending age (mofa), monastics were obsessed with profit and neglected the Way, thereby sinking into the cycle of birth and death, he was moved by such poignant grief and lamentation that he could not bear to remain silent.
He then composed this admonition to mutually warn, awaken, spur, and encourage one another. The record states:
*ya* (訝) means to sigh in astonishment; *jian* (緘) means to seal; *di* (遞) means to pass on in succession.

"What I regret is that we were born together in this Semblance Age (*nimitta-kalpa*). The time since the Sage departed is remote; the Buddha-dharma has become superficial, and many people are indolent.

The first two phrases lament not having encountered a sage-like era; the latter two phrases lament the degeneracy of the Dharma at its end and the stubbornness of men. As for "the Semblance Age": [it refers to the period following the True Dharma].
"End" (*ji*) refers to the final period. This is because the teachings of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, as they abide in the world, are divided into three periods:
the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), and the Final Dharma (*antima-dharma*). "True" (*zheng*) means "to verify" (*sākṣāt-kṛta*);

it refers to the first millennium after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during which those who receive the teaching are able to practice and thereby realize the fruit [of enlightenment]. "Semblance" (*xiang*) means "resembling."
It is said that there are both teachings and practices, resembling the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

This refers to the two thousand years following the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during which people who receive the teachings are able to practice them, yet for the most part are unable to realize the fruits [of the path]. As for "the Final Dharma" (*mappō*):

"final" (*matsu*) means the very end, or it also implies being minute and insignificant. This refers to the ten thousand years following the True and Semblance Dharma after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
The teachings have been transmitted to the world; yet although people receive these teachings, they are unable to practice them or realize the fruits of enlightenment.

Some say that the Dharma-ending age (mofa) lasts for thirty thousand years. Venerable Muzhou appeared during the Tang dynasty, approximately one thousand eight hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa;
thus it is called the "Semblance Age" (xiangji). Furthermore, he was nearly two thousand years removed from the Tathāgata; hence it is said that "the time is distant."
The times have become remote, and those great beings who transmit the Dharma gradually grow scarce; this is what is called being "unfamiliar.

Having lost excellent guides, we further encounter the final age (kalpa), when the faculties of sentient beings are inferior and lack the aspiration for the higher path; hence, it is called "indolence."

The Record states: Regarding the periods of Ji, Zhong, and Zhong, if one speaks in terms of the one thousand years of the Semblance Dharma (*sāṃketika-dharma*), the final three hundred years belong to the Ji period.
